Asked about temporary US sanctions waivers for Russian oil, Rubio said Washington had to juggle multiple factors “including our bilateral relationships with other countries and what they realistically are capable of being able to do in terms of their own energy supplies”.
“You also can’t unravel the economy of other countries because of one central issue,” he said.
The two countries reached an interim trade agreement in February aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian goods.
But days later, the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s sweeping tariffs, fuelling uncertainty over when the agreement would take effect.
The two sides have been negotiating ever since.
Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said this month the talks had reached “a plateau, beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult”.
Jaishankar met with his United Arab Emirates counterpart in Mumbai earlier on Tuesday. The UAE is a key supplier of Indian energy, especially liquefied natural gas (LNG).
“The situation in the Gulf remains a matter of deep concern,” Jaishankar told UAE Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, in public comments broadcast before their meeting started.
He said India continues to support “free, safe and unimpeded flow of trade, energy and fertiliser”.

title: Defamation tribunal orders Punjab Assembly opposition leader to pay Rs3m to Azma Bokhari
text:
LAHORE: The Punjab Defamation Tribunal on Tuesday ruled in favour of Punjab Information Minister Azma Bokhari in a defamation suit against Punjab Assembly Opposition Leader Moeen Riaz Qureshi, ordering him to pay Rs3 million in general damages.
In January, Bokhari filed the defamation suit against Qureshi seeking damages of Rs800 million. She filed the claim against the opposition leader, alleging that he made “baseless and fabricated” accusations against her.
In a short order issued on Tuesday, the tribunal said that the counsel for both parties had concluded their final arguments.
“The claim of the plaintiff is hereby decreed up to the extent of general damages amounting to Rupees three million (Rs3,000,000),” said tribunal member Anjum Raza Syed in an order seen by Dawn.
However, the tribunal dismissed the minister’s claim for special and punitive damages.
Meanwhile, the PTI said in its statement that its MPA was told to pay Rs84m in damages.
Bokhari’s counsel argued that the defendant, Qureshi, had acknowledged making the remarks in question during a television programme but had failed to produce any evidence to substantiate the allegations.
The tribunal said a detailed judgment would be issued separately.
The information minister had filed the suit following allegations Qureshi levelled at the time of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s then-chief minister Sohail Afridi’s visit to the Punjab Assembly.
He had alleged that the provincial minister got 200 paid individuals into the assembly premises, and that the journalists who put questions to Afridi were her salaried employees.
‘Attempt to respond to criticism with fines’
Commenting on the verdict, Qureshi wrote on X: “The voice I raise in favour of the people’s rights, the supremacy of the Constitution, and Imran Khan cannot be silenced.”
He asserted that as the opposition leader, his duty was “not to flatter those in power but to question them, defend the rights of the people, and stand firm against every undemocratic action”.
“Remember! Dissent is the strength of democracy, not its weakness. Attempting to respond to criticism with fines cannot prove any stance wrong.”
In its statement, the PTI expressed its deep concern over the verdict, assailing the Punjab government for being “unwilling to tolerate even political criticism and dissent”.
It contended that the PML-N introduced the Punjab Defamation Act 2024 and used its majority to turn it into law, which it has now employed.
Noting that Qureshi had been attempting to present a resolution in the Punjab Assembly against the imposition of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, PTI said the emergence of the verdict “raises questions about its timing and political implications”.

title: Maldives president arrives in Pakistan for three-day visit
text:
Maldives President Dr Mohamed Muizzu arrived in Islamabad on Tuesday on a three-day visit to Pakistan, according to a statement from his office.
Muizzu is visiting Pakistan at the invitation of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. The visit marks the first by a Maldivian president to Pakistan in 11 years, and comes as the two countries celebrate the 60th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations in 1966.
According to the statement, the Maldivian president and first lady were accorded a 21-gun salute upon their arrival at Islamabad International Airport.
“The president will be accorded an official welcome tomorrow at Prime Minister House, the official residence of the prime minister of Pakistan,” it added.
An earlier statement issued by the Foreign Office (FO) said Muizzu will meet President Asif Ali Zardari, who will host a state banquet in his honour.
He will also hold “restricted and delegation-level” talks with PM Shehbaz, the FO said.
During the talks, the two leaders will “review the entire spectrum of bilateral relations and explore avenues for further strengthening cooperation in trade, investment, health, education, tourism, agriculture, defence, maritime security, climate change and people-to-people exchanges”.
They will also exchange views on regional and international developments of mutual interest, according to the FO.
A Pakistan-Maldives Business Forum will also be held during the visit to promote interaction between the two countries’ business communities and explore opportunities for trade and investment.
“A number of agreements and memorandums of understanding (MoUs) covering diverse areas of bilateral cooperation are expected to be signed during the visit,” the statement added.
Meanwhile, the Maldivian delegation, led by Foreign Minister Iruthisham Adam and comprising cabinet ministers and senior officials, arrived in Islamabad earlier on Tuesday ahead of President Muizzu’s arrival, the Foreign Office (FO) said in a statement.
The delegation was received at the airport by the FO spokesperson, Director General (South Asia and Saarc), the Maldivian high commissioner to Pakistan and the Pakistani high commissioner to the Maldives.
In 2015, former Maldivian president Abdulla Yameen Abdul Gayoom undertook a two-day state visit to Pakistan on May 6-7 at the invitation of then-premier Nawaz Sharif.

title: Alberta votes to remain part of Canada
text:
Alberta residents voted to remain part of Canada in the province’s first-ever referendum on separation, in a much-needed win for Prime Minister Mark Carney as he attempts to unify the country amid a trade war with the US.
CBC News, Canada’s government-funded national broadcaster, called the result late Monday after 33 per cent of the vote had been counted. At the time of the call, 76pc of tallied votes were in support of the “remain” side versus 23pc in favour of the province moving forward with a binding vote on separation. The referendum was nonbinding.
“Albertans made a clear choice,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement.
“They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other.”
“Canada is greater than the sum of its parts,” he said.
Pollsters and analysts had repeatedly dismissed the possibility of a separatist victory, citing data that showed about one-third of residents in the western province supported a future referendum on leaving.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced the referendum in May, saying it was time to have a vote, understand the will of Albertans on this subject, and move on.
Late Monday, Smith issued a statement on social media saying she was “very pleased” that early results show widespread support for remaining in Canada. She said she would address Albertans on Tuesday to discuss the results and “where our province goes from here.”
A small but vocal group of separatists has campaigned for months for an independent Alberta, arguing that the province’s energy wealth is subsidising poorer parts of Canada and that Alberta would be far richer without Ottawa bureaucracy impeding its path.
Last week, Carney told a rally in Calgary that voting to leave Canada would be a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division, and appealed to Albertans to vote like Canada depends on it.
Carney, who grew up mostly in Alberta, acknowledged that Albertans have often felt slighted by Ottawa and said his government had approved a proposed new pipeline, adding that Alberta is critical to helping Canada reduce its dependence on the US.
Alberta’s referendum follows two previous referendums on separation in the majority French-speaking province of Quebec. Quebecers voted to stay in Canada in both instances.
First Nations groups have also objected to the idea of an independent Alberta, as their land treaties with Ottawa predate the province’s creation within Canada.
CBC News reported strong turnout from First Nations. One southern Alberta polling station in an area that is home to the Siksika Nation temporarily ran out of ballots, and then stayed open until after 10 pm MT (9 am PKT) to ensure everyone in line had the chance to vote.
Still, Monday’s referendum is unlikely to end the separatist movement in Alberta. Before the referendum, some separatist leaders said they would continue to pursue another vote even if most Albertans voted to remain.
According to data released on October 16 by the pollster Angus Reid, 62pc of Albertans believe there will never be an end to the separatist movement in the province.
Alberta’s referendum also included nine other nonbinding questions on topics including immigration, access to provincial services such as education, social care and healthcare and voter identification requirements. Results for those questions were still trickling in.

title: Health ministry gets Momin Agha as 9th secretary in 19 months
text:
ISLAMABAD: The health ministry has again gotten a new secretary, with the Establishment Division notifying Momin Agha as the new administrative head.
Agha, a BS-22 officer of the Pakistan Administrative Service (PAS), is the ninth secretary to be appointed during the tenure of Health Minister Mustafa Kamal, who took the oath in February 2025.
According to a notification issued by the Establishment Division on Monday, available with Dawn, Agha “has been transferred and posted as secretary health with immediate effect and until further orders”.
A health expert, requesting anonymity, said eight officers had held the post during the past 19 months, with some changes involving repeat appointments.
According to him, Nadeem Mahboob remained till March 2025, Nasiruddin Mashood till May 2025, Waqarul Hasan till June 2025, Hamed Yaqoob till Feb 2026, Aslam Ghauri till August 2026, retired Captain Mahmood till Sept 2026, then Fakhre Alam joined, and later Mahboob got additional charge of the ministry for just one day before he was replaced with Agha.
When contacted earlier, Kamal had told Dawn that he had nothing to do with the changes of secretaries, as the Establishment Division was empowered to make such decisions.
Agha was removed as petroleum secretary in January 2026 and directed to report to the Establishment Division without a further posting.
He was replaced by Mirza Nasiruddin Ahmad, who was given the additional charge of the post on a look-after basis pending the appointment of a regular officer.

title: France to impose new curfews where necessary: PM
text:
France will impose new curfews in areas where needed on Tuesday, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said, adding that the measures introduced in several cities the previous day had “helped keep the night calm”.
France was rocked on Saturday by some of its worst rioting in recent years, just six months before the country elects a successor to President Emmanuel Macron.
Accused of failing to anticipate and contain the street violence, the government has pledged to restore order, and had announced partial curfews in Paris and some other cities on Monday.
“Targeted curfews have contributed to calm overnight,” Lecornu wrote on X.
“Tonight new curfews will be decided where the situation requires it. These decisions will be made on the ground, by the prefects, in coordination with the mayors,” he said.
Police confirmed the night had passed without major incidents across France.
Several cities, including Paris, the southwestern city of Bordeaux and Nice on the French Riviera, introduced partial curfews on Monday in response to urban unrest that followed weeks of student demonstrations over poor learning conditions in high schools.
While some restrictions, such as those in Paris, initially applied only for the night from Monday to Tuesday, others, particularly in Bordeaux and Nice, were set to remain in force for several days.
During the night, a helicopter flew over the French capital’s Place de la Republique, one of the epicentres of the unrest, sweeping a powerful searchlight across the square to monitor compliance with the curfew.
In Lyon, despite a ban on demonstrations, around 500 people gathered on Monday evening outside the tourism office that was set on fire, to show support for shopkeepers affected by looting, according to organisers.
The word “LYON” had been spelled out on the ground with candles.
A banner hung on a fence nearby read “Anti-Rioters Lyon” and “Doucet Resign”, referring to Green mayor Gregory Doucet, an AFP journalist said.
Under pressure, the government scheduled another series of emergency meetings on Tuesday, including talks involving representatives of major social media platforms.
Finance Minister Roland Lescure pledged support measures for shopkeepers and craftspeople.
Patrick Martin, the head of France’s Medef business lobby group, on Tuesday accused the state of having “failed” during the urban unrest that hit at least 3,000 businesses, according to preliminary estimates.

title: Pakistan, Qatar agree to strengthen internal security cooperation
text:
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi and his Qatari counterpart, Sheikh Khalifa bin Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, have agreed to strengthen bilateral cooperation in internal security, according to a statement issued by the Interior Ministry on Tuesday.
The two met in Doha and held a detailed exchange of views on enhancing cooperation in internal security, the statement said.
They also discussed the current regional situation and matters relating to peace and stability.
“The meeting reaffirmed the commitment to strengthening bilateral cooperation between the two interior ministries,” the statement said, adding that a decision was made to strengthen mutual cooperation and partnership in internal security.
The meeting came a day after Naqvi addressed the 8th Global Security Forum in Doha, where he said Pakistan and Qatar had worked together to promote regional peace and stability.
He recalled the Lake Lucerne Summit in Switzerland, organised by Pakistan and Qatar to facilitate US-Iran talks.
Praising Qatar’s role in the peace efforts, Naqvi said the two countries’ aim was to “stop further conflict and to save innocent lives”.
“In the diplomacy of our time, when others chose sides, Qatar chose to keep talking. Pakistan has seen this closely because we have worked beside you,” he said.
Naqvi last met Al Thani on July 28 in Doha, where the two discussed security cooperation and ways to further strengthen bilateral relations in the security sector.

title: ECONOMY: The Missing Entrepreneur of Sindh
text:
During a recent visit to Borneo island in the Malay archipelago, I came across a shrimp farm on the coast of the rainforest-covered island, run by a Chinese woman entrepreneur. Using a seawater reservoir behind a mangrove forest, she had built a business exporting shrimp around the world.
My mind drifted home to Pakistan’s 1,058-kilometre coastline, along Sindh and Balochistan. Why, I wondered, do we see so little aquaculture of this kind?
I was reminded of a conversation I had with the owner of a hatchery recently established in Gharo in Sindh. He told me that one of his biggest worries was transporting the hatchlings quickly and safely to fish and shrimp farms in Muzaffargarh, Punjab.
The irony struck me. The hatchery is in coastal Sindh, close to the sea and the Indus delta, yet its young fish and shrimp have to travel hundreds of kilometres inland to find farms. I asked him why people were not investing in fish and shrimp farming in Sindh? He did not have a clear answer, except to say that there were not enough investors and the business climate is also not supportive.
But the lack of investors is not really an explanation. It is itself a question.
The problem in rural Sindh may not be a lack of capital, but its concentration — and the failure to create the conditions in which small businesses can grow into industries
Sindh has fertile land, a long coastline and a river, alongside abundant agricultural produce, livestock, fisheries and traditional crafts. Yet much of this potential has not translated into local processing, packaging and cold-chain businesses that could create jobs beyond agriculture. Why did this not happen?
THE AGRARIAN DIVIDE
Economic historian Imran Ali has documented how British canal colonies transformed western Punjab from the late 19th century. Irrigation brought semi-arid land under cultivation, encouraging commercial agriculture and the growth of new settlements and market towns. The colonial project also served revenue, political and military objectives. Regardless of their motives, the economic landscape was transformed.
Sindh too underwent an irrigation revolution, particularly after the Sukkur Barrage opened in 1932. But perhaps the social structure on to which this new agricultural wealth was grafted was different.
Economist Mahmood Hasan Khan points out the growth of small owner-cultivators and market relations in parts of Punjab, while the older landlord-sharecropper structure remained much stronger in Sindh. Economist Akmal Hussain argues that owner-cultivators have greater incentives to invest, potentially generating the savings and demand needed for industrialisation.
Where agricultural income is concentrated in fewer hands, the pattern of investment may be different.
THE CONCENTRATION OF CAPITAL
It would, however, be too easy to explain Sindh’s predicament simply by invoking “feudalism.”
Political economist Akbar Zaidi argues that agriculture in Pakistan has undergone a substantial capitalist transformation. Commercialisation and the ‘Green Revolution’ brought capitalist farmers, machinery and wage labour and, in some areas, small manufacturers, skilled workers and service businesses.
Sindh’s sugar mills, cotton ginning and rice milling show that agricultural wealth did become industrial capital. But large enterprises owned by wealthy families are not the same as a broad base of independent businesses. Both represent investment and capitalism, but the latter creates a much wider entrepreneurial class.
A farmer investing in transport, a workshop repairing agricultural machinery or a manufacturer producing spare parts can generate further demand for suppliers, traders and services. Why has this chain remained so weak across much of rural Sindh?
THE CITY AND THE HINTERLAND
Perhaps the problem was never simply the absence of capital. It may have been the concentration of capital and the failure to spread entrepreneurial investment widely enough through its towns and communities.
And then there is Karachi. Economist Kaiser Bengali has described Sindh as having a “dual identity”: Karachi on one side and the rest of the province on the other.
Partition created another rupture. Much of Sindh’s Hindu mercantile and entrepreneurial class migrated to India, while Muslim migrants from different parts of the Subcontinent brought new commercial skills, networks and capital to Karachi. Over the following decades, Karachi became Pakistan’s great port, financial centre and industrial metropolis. For someone from rural Sindh with money to invest, a good education or entrepreneurial ability, Karachi offered far greater opportunities than his own town.
Perhaps herein lies another paradox. Sindh generated considerable wealth at both ends of its economy: agricultural wealth in the countryside and commercial and industrial wealth in Karachi. Yet the economic centres in between remained relatively weak.
BEYOND INDUSTRIAL ESTATES
History, however, can only explain so much. Nearly eight decades have passed since Independence, and we also have to ask what we have done since then. Why have Sukkur, Larkana, Nawabshah, Mirpurkhas, Khairpur, Thatta and Badin not developed stronger clusters of small industry?
Industrial estates and special economic zones have been established or proposed outside Karachi, but infrastructure alone does not create an industrial ecosystem. Regional businesses also need technical training, accessible finance, shared processing and testing facilities, and reliable market connections.
Perhaps the more fundamental question is why we wait for investors instead of creating the conditions that produce investors.
THE MISSING STEP
A recent article by journalist Owais Tohid about thousands of women establishing tiny businesses across rural Sindh provides an interesting clue. These women are raising livestock, stitching clothes, producing handicrafts and running other small businesses with relatively modest amounts of capital.
Perhaps entrepreneurship was never absent. The problem is what happens next. How does a woman employing herself begin employing five or ten other women? How does a workshop become a factory? How does one successful shrimp farm become twenty, surrounded by hatcheries, feed suppliers, cold storage, processors, transporters and exporters?
This brings me back to that hatchery in Gharo. The coastline is there, as are the seawater, the hatchery, the technical knowledge and the market. And yet the hatchlings travel hundreds of kilometres to find the entrepreneurs willing and able to farm them.
Successive governments in Sindh must also bear part of the responsibility. A political economy historically dominated by large landowners may not have had sufficient incentive to create a broad class of independent entrepreneurs.
Industrial estates have been established, but we have rarely pursued industrial development around the natural strengths of individual regions with the persistence it requires: dates in Khairpur, fisheries and aquaculture along the coast, rice in upper Sindh, fruit processing around Mirpurkhas, and livestock and dairy across much of the province.
Nor can poverty alleviation alone be an economic policy. There is an obvious need for social protection in a province where millions remain poor. But cash support, however necessary, cannot by itself create economic mobility. The larger challenge is to create the conditions in which people can move beyond poverty.
A tenant becoming an owner, a woman running a tiny business beginning to employ others, a workshop growing into a factory, or a farmer’s produce being processed and packaged before it leaves the district rather than being sent elsewhere for someone else to add value to it — these are perhaps better measures of economic development.
The challenge for rural Sindh, therefore, may not simply be to find more investors. It is to understand why enterprise has failed to spread despite the province’s considerable natural resources and agricultural wealth, and then to create the conditions in which capital, skills and entrepreneurship can come together.
Ultimately, the measure of development should not merely be how many poor people the state is able to support, but how many people are able to reach a point where they no longer need that support.
The writer is an entrepreneur and President of WWF-Pakistan
Published in Dawn, EOS, October 18th, 2026

title: Toll on trade
text:
A YEAR after Islamabad severed commercial ties with Kabul over security concerns, the border trade disruption is taking a growing toll on KP, where livelihoods, businesses, farm markets, and a large number of workers depend on cross-border commerce. Bilateral trade has fallen by more than 72pc, from $1.3bn in FY25 to $358m in FY26 — which means fewer customers for local shops, lower earnings for farmers, idle trucks, and lost jobs.
KP was already struggling to attract investment and create work amid rising terrorism; the loss of an established market makes recovery harder. The damage is not confined to the province. Farmers and factories in Punjab and Sindh, too, have been hit, and Pakistan’s exports to Central Asia have been badly disrupted.
Afghanistan has long been KP’s natural outlet because of its proximity and the long-standing commercial and tribal networks. Traders built their businesses around moving food, cement, pharmaceuticals, and other goods across the border. Medical tourism, hotels, and other services catering to Afghan visitors are suffering as well. When crossings shut, traders cannot send their goods to distant markets without facing higher costs, finding new buyers, and adapting to unfamiliar commercial conditions.
In fact, most services cannot be shifted at all. Rerouting shipments is not an easy fix. Pakistan’s shortest land routes to Central Asia run through Afghanistan. Alternatives mean longer distances, higher freight costs, and thinner margins. Small enterprises with little financial cushion are the most exposed to prolonged border trade closures.
KP needs expanding markets and productive investment to employ a growing workforce; it cannot afford to lose existing ones before alternatives are in place. Islamabad has valid security concerns — the Taliban must prevent Afghan territory from being used for attacks on Pakistan. But border closures also hurt citizens on both sides, who have nothing to do with Kabul’s policies.
Islamabad must find the right balance between its security priorities and the economic strain on KP’s residents. Sustained efforts to obtain genuine security assurances from Kabul and carefully monitored arrangements for legitimate trade may offer a way to protect both. It should also assess the losses of traders, transporters, and farmers, and help businesses find new markets. The government must protect its people from terrorism without restricting their livelihoods.
Published in Dawn, October 20th, 2026

title: Health authorities dismiss reports of insulin shortage, cite unavailability of one brand
text:
ISLAMABAD: Authorities on Tuesday denied reports of a widespread insulin shortage in the country, saying that only one brand was unavailable due to international supply constraints.
The clarification came after reports of a shortage across Pakistan emerged on social media.
The health ministry and the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (Drap) maintained that alternatives for the unavailable brand remained available in the market.
“Insulin glulisine (Apidra, Sanofi) is currently unavailable due to international supply constraints. Alternate rapid-acting analogues within the same pharmacological class, specifically insulin aspart (NovoRapid, Novo Nordisk) and insulin lispro (Humalog, Eli Lilly), are readily available nationwide,” ministry spokesperson Sajid Shah said.
“All other primary insulin classes remain fully accessible across Pakistan,” he added.
He explained that insulin analogues — one of the two categories of medically approved insulin — include rapid-acting, long-acting and premixed formulations. The other category, human insulin, includes short-acting and intermediate-acting formulations.
The spokesperson added that patients who have been prescribed Apidra “should consult their attending healthcare provider prior to modifying their regimen”.
“Any transition to an alternative insulin formulation requires precise dose titration and tailored monitoring to maintain optimal glycaemic control,” he said.
In August 2025, the Pakistan Medical Association (PMA) raised alarm over “an unprecedented” and severe shortage of essential medicines across the country and warned that the crisis threatened the lives of millions of patients.
According to the association, at least 80 important medicines were unavailable, with 25 having no substitutes. These drugs included life-saving medications for diabetes, cancer, Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, heart disease and psychiatric disorders.
In March 2026, PMA cautioned about the severe shortage of essential paediatric tuberculosis (TB) as well as cancer medications, warning that the humanitarian crisis was getting worse with each passing day, while calling for immediate intervention.

title: US bars IT firm from sponsoring green cards, imposes $2m settlement
text:
WASHINGTON: The United States has barred California-based technology company Cloudera Inc. from participating in the employment-based green card process for two years and secured a $2 million settlement over allegations that it discriminated against qualified American workers.
The settlement was announced jointly by the US Department of Justice and the Department of Labour. It resolves a lawsuit filed by the Justice Department in April, alleging that Cloudera violated the Immigration and Nationality Act by discriminating against American workers while recruiting for seven positions under the Permanent Labour Certification, or PERM, programme.
Under the settlement, Cloudera will establish a $1.4m fund to compensate qualified US workers who tried to apply for the positions but were not given fair consideration. The company will also pay $600,000 in civil penalties to the US government.
“There are no exceptions: the Justice Department will hold accountable employers who discriminate against US workers,” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division said.
The warning has wider implications for future employment-based green card applications. Employers found to have discriminated against qualified American workers could face penalties and restrictions on their ability to sponsor foreign employees, potentially disrupting the permanent residency plans of those workers.
The Cloudera case demonstrates how enforcement action against an employer can directly affect foreign professionals seeking green cards through company sponsorship. The company will also face enhanced monitoring, revised compliance procedures and reporting requirements designed to prevent future violations.
The two-year debarment follows an earlier suspension of Cloudera’s PERM processing by the Labour Department. During the debarment period, the company cannot participate in the PERM programme to sponsor foreign workers for employment-based green cards.
The PERM programme is generally the first major step when a US employer seeks to sponsor a foreign worker for an employment-based green card under the EB-2 or EB-3 categories.
Employers must normally demonstrate that no qualified, willing and available American workers could be found for the position and that employing the foreign worker would not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed US workers.
According to the allegations, Cloudera’s recruitment for seven positions did not give qualified American workers a fair opportunity to compete. Applicants were reportedly directed to an email address that did not accept messages from outside senders, potentially preventing them from submitting applications.
The decision is relevant to Indian and Pakistani professionals seeking US permanent residency through employer sponsorship, but it does not impose a general ban on green cards for nationals of either country.
Cloudera-sponsored applications could face disruption. Employees whose green card cases depend on the company’s labour certification may face delays or need to explore lawful alternatives, depending on their individual circumstances and the stage of their cases. The debarment does not, by itself, establish that every existing green card application sponsored by Cloudera will be cancelled.
The settlement also underscores the potential consequences for employers that fail to provide American workers a genuine opportunity to compete for jobs. Depending on the findings and enforcement action in an individual case, such employers could face financial penalties, compliance requirements or restrictions on their participation in employment-based immigration programmes.
However, the wider immigration rules remain unchanged. The settlement does not alter employment-based visa eligibility, annual numerical limits or country-specific visa allocation rules.
The Justice Department said the Cloudera settlement was the 14th since it relaunched its Protecting US Workers Initiative in 2025. The initiative targets employers accused of unlawfully favouring foreign workers holding temporary employment visas over qualified American workers.
The case underscores the importance of fair recruitment practices in the green card sponsorship process. Employers must provide American workers a genuine opportunity to apply before seeking labour certification for foreign employees.
On October 8, the Trump administration froze some green-card filings by Microsoft, Adobe and major IT outsourcers and opened probes into nine elite universities, widening a visa crackdown it said targets fraud and American job losses.

title: Govt unveils hi-tech system to manage loadshedding
text:
• Asset Performance Management System pilot project to be launched from Lahore, Kasur
• APMS to be synced with smart meters to monitor power consumption in real-time
• System will help authorities triangulate point of loss, theft with greater accuracy
LAHORE: The government is all set to introduce the Asset Performance Management System (APMS), also known as the Advanced Power Management System, to control power theft and load management across the country in a phased manner.
Minister for Energy (Power Division) Awais Leghari, while speaking at a ceremony in Dera Ghazi Khan on Monday, revealed the government’s plan to introduce modern technology to combat power theft and curtail line losses. According to him, the APMS will identify specific transformers in high-theft areas, enabling targeted disconnections so that thousands of paying consumers on an entire feeder are not penalised for the actions of electricity thieves.
The minister reiterated that loadshedding will continue on feeders reporting 30 percent or higher losses, emphasising that no leniency will be shown toward electricity thieves or chronic defaulters.
According to power experts, the APMS will enable more targeted identification of high-loss consumers, improve energy accounting, enhance operational visibility, and support equitable load management through data-driven decision-making.
As the Power Planning and Monitoring Company (PPMC), the technical arm of the Ministry of Energy (Power Division), is playing a central role in supporting the planning, design, and effective implementation of this sector-wide reform, the APMS will serve as a key enabler in achieving these objectives through transformer-level monitoring, analytics, digital oversight, and enforcement mechanisms across Discos.
The APMS works alongside Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) and Automated Meter Reading (AMR) rollouts, enabling two-way communication and remote cutoff capabilities. “The APMS pilot project is all set to be launched in Lahore and Kasur soon, as the necessary work is underway by the Lahore Electric Supply Company (Lesco). Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif will inaugurate this pilot project soon,” confirmed an official source in Lesco while talking to Dawn.
Talking about the background and launch of the APMS, he said the Discos have been implementing, for the last few years, the Power Division’s policy under which loadshedding is observed, keeping in view the loss category of 11kV feeders.
According to him, loadshedding (both scheduled and forced) is being observed at loss-making feeders categorised as 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5. Two hours of loadshedding are observed in areas falling within the service jurisdiction of category-1 feeders, followed by four, six, eight, and 10 hours on category 2, 3, 4, and 5 feeders, respectively.
“The problem is that if we observe loadshedding in the areas falling within the service jurisdiction of such loss-making feeders, all consumers, including those paying their bills regularly, also bear the brunt of those stealing electricity. So this system will soon be in place, gradually, to protect the rights of law-abiding consumers,” he explained.
He said that under the new arrangement, the APMS would be installed on transformers of various capacities currently placed on poles.
After the APMS installations, the existing conventional electricity meters would be replaced by AMI meters (smart meters).
After replacement, the APMS would be synced with the smart meters and start monitoring the real-time consumption of electricity users.
“Suppose there are 200 consumers receiving power from one transformer in any area. The APMS at each transformer will record the total number of units received from the power distribution system and the actual number of units used by the consumers.
If the units received from the system are 100,000 and the number used by the consumers is less than that, it would mean that the remaining units have been stolen through unfair means. In this way, it will be easy for the Discos to detect power-stealing consumers,” he explained.
“At present, it is difficult to detect power thieves in a vast area (2,000 to 3,000 consumers or even more) covered by a feeder. With the APMS, the area would be narrowed from the feeder to the transformer (150 to 200 consumers),” he said, adding that this would help Lesco stop power theft and reduce line losses more effectively. According to another Lesco officer, the APMS would be installed in a 2/4-foot iron box at transformers. “The APMS would automatically report the theft, line losses, etc. to the officials concerned, enabling them to respond quickly to fix the issue,” he maintained. Similarly, he said, if someone touched the AMI meter with the intention to tamper with it and steal electricity, the meter itself would report to the system monitored by the officials.
Published in Dawn, October 20th, 2026

title: GDP growth revised down to 3.65pc as country falls short of target
text:
• Industrial, services sector slowdown drags down economic growth in FY26
• Per capita income ‘lowest in region’; economy reaches $450.4bn
ISLAMABAD: The government on Monday revised the gross domestic product (GDP) growth slightly downward to 3.65 per cent for the outgoing fiscal year (FY26), attributing the adjustment to a mild slowdown in the industrial and services sectors.
The country’s GDP registered modest growth alongside an increase in per capita income in dollar terms, reflecting a sluggish pace of recovery in the country’s overall output compared with the previous year, the government said.
In May 2026, the government had projected the economy to grow by 3.70pc in FY26, revising its earlier estimate of 4pc. The downward adjustment now indicates that the country fell short of its GDP target.
The revised growth rates in agriculture, industry and services in FY26 are 3.50pc, 3.34pc and 3.81pc, respectively, compared with earlier growth rates of 2.89pc, 3.51pc and 4.09pc.
The revision came during the 118th meeting of the National Accounts Committee (NAC), which was held on Monday at the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics.
The NAC estimate places Pakistan broadly in line with the outlook of multilateral lenders, though with some variation.
The International Monetary Fund has projected GDP growth at 3.6pc for FY26, the World Bank at 3.7pc and the Asian Development Bank at 3.7pc, while the State Bank of Pakistan expects growth to remain close to 3.7pc.
The committee approved the incorporation of revised imports data in the national accounts estimates from FY21 to FY25, quarterly GDP growth rates for Q1 (revised), Q2 (revised), Q3 (revised), and Q4 during FY26 and updated annual growth rates for FY25 and FY26.
The size of the economy rose to $450.4 billion in FY26 from $410.96bn in FY25, mainly driven by growth in the services sector, followed by industry and livestock.
Per capita income slightly increased to $1,896 in FY26, the lowest in the region, up from $1,824 in FY25. The projection is based on the 2023 census. However, it was $1,551 in FY23, $1,766 in FY22 and $1,677 in FY21.
This suggests a deterioration in the standard of living and well-being across almost all segments of society, with no tangible increase in personal incomes due to unprecedented inflationary pressures, which reduce disposable income and limit individuals’ ability to afford goods and services, save, or invest.
Updated growth rates
Meanwhile, the NAC also approved the updated growth rates for Q1, Q2 and Q3 of 2025-26 at 3.89pc, 4.31pc and 4.42pc, respectively, compared with 3.92pc, 4.05pc and 3.99pc, presented at the 117th meeting of the NAC. The fourth quarter of FY26 recorded a 2pc growth in GDP. The committee approved the updated annual growth of 3.11pc for FY25, which was estimated at 3.18pc in the previous meeting.
In agriculture, important crops improved from 0.65pc to 1.59pc due to wheat and maize, other crops have witnessed significant improvement from 2.43pc to 4.28pc due to higher production of pulses (6.3pc), fruits (1.3pc), tomato (44pc), oilseed (5.4pc), and green fodder (2.4pc). Livestock decreased slightly from 3.75pc to 3.71pc because of increased fodder inputs. Updated growth rates in forestry and fishing are 10.80pc and 1.39pc, respectively.
The committee revised growth in industry during FY26 to 3.34pc from 3.51pc estimated previously. The mining & quarrying industry has improved from 0.38pc to 1.52pc due to improvement in gas (2.84pc), crude oil (5.12pc), and coal (2.73pc). Large-scale manufacturing (LSM), which is measured through the Quantum Index of Manufacturing (QIM), has declined from 6.11pc to 5.01pc.
The major LSM groups with positive contributions are food (7.03pc), tobacco (12.61pc), petroleum products (9.7pc), rubber products (14.19pc), electrical equipment (14.25pc), automobiles (57.77pc), transport equipment (42.36pc), furniture (22.69pc), and other manufacturing (football) (16.62pc). The construction industry has improved from 5.73pc to 6.30pc because of increased construction-related expenditure in the public sector.
However, some LSM groups posted negative growth, e.g., pharmaceuticals (-8.87pc), iron & steel products (-7.84pc), chemicals (-2.53pc), and leather products (-1.95pc), electricity (-10.24pc) in FY26.
The services industry has declined from 4.09pc to 3.81pc in FY26, with positive contributions from all the constituents. The growth in wholesale and retail trade posted at 2.37pc as against the previous growth of 3.71pc due to decrease in manufacturing and imports.
Transport and storage industry growth improved to 3.23pc from 2.31pc due to upward revisions reported in railways, water transport, and air transport. Similarly, information & communication growth increased from 7.52pc to 9.53pc, the finance & insurance also improved from 0.32pc to 4.23pc in FY26 due to improvement in the insurance industry.
The slowdown was also reported in public administration and social security to 5.67pc from 8.54pc, education 4.17pc from 5.23pc, and human health and social work 5.52pc from 6.85pc.
Published in Dawn, October 20th, 2026

title: Houthis inflict major losses on Yemeni forces
text:
• At least 53 killed, 200 wounded in attack on govt forces’ training camp in Shabwa
• Egypt delays vote on military support for Saudi Arabia
• US embassies urge ‘heightened vigilance’ across region; Riyadh residents get ‘hostile aerial threat’ warning; govt staff told to work from home
• ‘Davos in the Desert’ postponed to next year
RIYADH: At least 53 people were killed and 200 others injured on Monday in a Houthi attack on a government security forces training camp in Yemen’s Shabwa province, local authorities said, as fighting in the impoverished country intensifies.
Local sources, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the Houthis launched three ballistic missiles at security forces during a training exercise. Video from Shabwa province verified by Reuters showed injured people and bloodied bodies scattered across the ground.
The attack came amid escalating hostilities between the Houthis and Yemen’s internationally recognised government, backed by a Saudi-led coalition, with both sides trading attacks since the group advanced in September toward territory near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a strategic shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea.
The fighting in Yemen has become another front in the wider US-Israeli war with Iran, as the Houthis step up attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest crude oil exporter.
Riyadh alerts
Saudi authorities on Monday issued brief phone alerts to residents of the capital, Riyadh, and the nearby Kharj area, warning of a “hostile aerial threat”.
“A warning has been issued by the National Early Warning Platform in Riyadh City to alert of a potential danger,” Saudi civil defence said in a statement on X.
Hours later, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for six military operations over 48 hours using ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones.
Saree said the attacks targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu on the Red Sea coast and the Shaybah oil field near the United Arab Emirates border.
Other strikes targeted Abha International Airport, radar installations and Khamis Mushait air base in the southwest, alongside a naval camp and radar site in Bir Askar in the south.
Saree claimed the three-stage attack on the Riyadh airport achieved “accurate and direct” strikes in retaliation for more than 200 Saudi airstrikes and missile attacks on Houthi-held areas over the previous 48 hours.
He vowed to continue operations “towards the Saudi interior” under a policy of “escalation for escalation” until attacks on Yemen cease.
Work from home
Amid the repeated cross-border strikes, government agencies in Riyadh instructed employees to work from home starting from Monday, according to a worker and two consultants who spoke to AFP.
An internal message sent on Sunday evening said, “It has been decided to implement remote work from Monday to Thursday this week,” while asking staff to “continue their activities as normal”.
Meanwhile, the 99-storey Kingdom Centre in downtown Riyadh, which houses the regional office of the International Monetary Fund, asked employees to stay away until further notice.
Companies in the King Abdullah Financial District, home to major American firms, issued similar remote-work directives, while government offices in central Riyadh’s Al-Olaya district were evacuated two weeks earlier.
The worsening security situation prompted US embassies across the Gulf, Israel, Iraq, Lebanon and Jordan to urge the Americans on Monday to exercise heightened vigilance eight months into the US-Iran war.
“Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance due to the complex security environment,” the security alert said, warning of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions.
Noting that Riyadh’s international airport remained closed, the alert warned that “the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area” and urged citizens to prepare contingency plans.
Vote delayed, conference postponed
As regional concerns mount, Egypt’s parliament postponed until Oct 26 a vote on authorising the armed forces to support Saudi Arabia if requested.
Lawmakers adjourned a second closed-door session on Monday to discuss President Abdel Fattah el-Sissi’s request for authority to back the kingdom.
While el-Sissi said on Saturday that Egypt would take “any measure” necessary to protect its Gulf allies, the Egyptian Social Democratic Party instructed its lawmakers to abstain, citing economic pressures, risks to Suez Canal revenue and insufficient information on the mission’s scope and risks.
The escalating conflict has also disrupted Saudi Arabia’s business calendar, prompting organisers on Monday to postpone the flagship Future Investment Initiative conference until 2027.
Scheduled for Oct 26-29 and informally known as “Davos in the Desert,” the 10th edition of the state-backed event was set to feature executives including Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon, Standard Chartered CEO Bill Winters and Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser.
While organisers said the postponement would ensure the event delivered “the full scale, extraordinary quality, and unforgettable impact that our community has come to expect”, Semafor reported that major financial firms had privately conveyed safety concerns to Saudi Public Investment Fund Governor Yasir Al-Rumayyan.
Published in Dawn, October 20th, 2026

title: Peshawar High Court hears petitions against governor’s rule today
text:
PESHAWAR: With Peshawar High Court set to hear today (Tuesday) multiple petitions against imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, PTI chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan has sought permission of the court to file an amended petition to challenge the resolutions passed by a joint sitting of the Parliament as well as National Assembly and Senate separately endorsing the said move.
According to the cause list released by the high court, a two-member bench comprising the senior puisne judge, Justice Ijaz Anwar, and Justice Mohammad Faheem Wali will hear seven constitutional petitions, requesting the court to declare as unconstitutional the Oct 11 presidential proclamation under articles 232 and 234 imposing emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
The main petition is that of Barrister Gohar Ali, whereas leaders of Tehreek-i-Tahafuz Ayeen-i-Pakistan (TTAP) including its chairman Mahmood Khan Achakzai, its vice chairman Raja Nasir Abbas, Balochistan National Party (Mengal) chief Sardar Akhtar Mengal, Sindh United Party president Zainul Abideen and others have filed two petitions.
Barrister Gohar seeks permission to file amended petition to also challenge parliamentary resolutions endorsing govt move
The other petitions are that of National Democratic Movement’s central and provincial presidents Mohsin Dawar and Bushra Gohar, MNA Shandana Gulzar, and lawyers Suleman Khan and Qaiser Ali Shah.
The petitioners will be represented by Barrister Sameer Khosa, Salman Akram Raja, Ali
Zaman, Mohammad Yousaf Orakzai, Bassam Ahmad Siddiqui, Suleman Khan and Qaiser Shah, etc.
The federal government on Oct 11 imposed emergency in KP, and placed the province under governor’s rule, taking note of the ‘provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism’.
The move followed weeks of political tensions between the Centre and PTI – as well as negotiations to bridge their differences – after the latter announced a protest march to Islamabad to demand the release of its jailed founder Imran Khan.
Barrister Gohar on Monday filed an application in the high court, seeking permission to add two further prayers in his constitutional petition.
He requested the court to permit him to make consequential amendments to the facts and grounds of the petition and to file an amended petition within such time as the court may fix.
The prayers which Barrister Gohar requested for inclusion in his petition are: “Declare that the impugned resolutions, namely the separate resolutions passed by National Assembly and Senate on 14 Oct, 2026, and the resolutions passed by Majlis-i-Shoora (Parliament) in joint sitting on 15 Oct, 2026, approving the impugned proclamation, and the impugned SRO are unconstitutional,
without lawful authority and of no legal effect insofar as they approve, sustain or give effect to the impugned proclamation, and do not validate the impugned proclamation or any action taken under it.”
He also requested to “suspend the operation of the impugned SRO and restrain the respondents from taking any further step pursuant to the impugned resolutions or the impugned SRO.”
The application was filed by Advocate Shah Faisal Ilyas on behalf of Mr Gohar.
The applicant stated that on Oct 14 the National Assembly and the Senate passed separate resolutions approving the proclamation of emergency “under second proviso of clause (1) of Article 232”.
He stated that on Oct 15 the Parliament in a joint sitting passed two further resolutions, the first approving the proclamation of emergency under clause (7) of Article 232, and the second approving the proclamation under clause (3) of Article 234. He added that a consequential SRO was also issued by the government announcing the passage of the said resolutions.
“The proclamation of emergency has purportedly been approved by each of the impugned resolutions. Since these are subsequent developments and seek to clothe the inherently unlawful and unconstitutional impugned proclamation with legality, the petitioner is aggrieved of the same,” he said.
Published in Dawn, October 20th, 2026

title: Govt slashes petrol price by Rs5.16 per litre, high-speed diesel rate by Rs7.69
text:
The government on Monday cut the price of petrol by Rs5.16 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs7.69.
Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs381.14 per litre while HSD will cost Rs389.27 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.
According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable for Oct 20 (Tuesday).
The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28.
The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.
Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months.
On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “relief scheme” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices.
Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.
Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel.
The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.
Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.
Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.
Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

title: PM warns against resistance to FBR reforms
text:
ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Monday warned tax officers that resistance to the ongoing reforms in the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) would not be tolerated, directing the authorities to implement proposed measures to minimise the country’s tax gap.
The prime minister’s warning came during a weekly briefing on tax reforms, following a call for a pen-down strike by the Inland Revenue Officers Association. The strike call was later withdrawn after intervention by senior FBR officials. FBR Chairman Rashid Mahmood Langrial briefed the prime minister on the pilot project for faceless assessment and audit.
A source privy to the meeting told Dawn that the prime minister expressed displeasure over the strike announcement. “We will not tolerate any resistance against the ongoing reforms in the FBR,” PM Shehbaz was quoted as saying, adding that officers unwilling to work would be asked to leave.
The prime minister reminded tax officers that their salaries had been increased fourfold and that they had been provided with vehicles and accommodation. “We have extended every facility to these officers,” he said, adding that it was now their responsibility to deliver results and justify the incentives granted to them.
The FBR has established the National Faceless Centre (NFC) in Islamabad, where dedicated wings will handle audits and assessments through a faceless system aimed at reducing official discretion and direct contact between tax officials and taxpayers.
Initially staffed by 27 officers, the centre has been tasked with auditing and assessing third-party data relating to 300,000 to 400,000 individuals under a pilot project that became effective on October 1. The data will be referred to the NFC in phases after the completion of initial compliance checks.
According to an official announcement by the Prime Minister’s Secretariat, PM Shehbaz directed that the pace of FBR reforms be accelerated, noting that the initial results of the ongoing measures were encouraging.
He emphasised that the institution’s capacity must be continuously strengthened to bridge the tax gap.
The prime minister directed the FBR chairman to expedite the rollout of the faceless system in tax collection. “These reforms are in the larger interest of the state and will continue under all circumstances,” he said, adding that indiscriminate action should be taken against corrupt officials.
He further directed that officers and staff showing improvements in conduct and performance be given opportunities to reform, while those persisting in corruption and inefficiency would have no place in the organisation.
Meanwhile, the FBR suspended two Inland Revenue Service officers, one in BS-20 and the other in BS-19, and repatriated two other BS-20 officers to FBR Headquarters for further investigation over an unauthorised press statement and a call to suspend official work.
Published in Dawn, October 20th, 2026

title: KP has vast potential for industrial growth: governor
text:
PESHAWAR: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi on Monday said the province had vast potential for industrial development, so there was a need for a comprehensive and practical strategy to fully explore it for creating employment and strengthening the provincial economy.
He was chairing a meeting of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Economic Zones Development and Management Company (EZDMC) at Governor House here.
Officials briefed the governor on the EZDMC’s administrative structure, performance, achievements, future targets, economic zones, revenue generation and other related matters.
Adviser to the governor on industries Mohammad Irshad, secretary of the industries department and other senior officials attended the meeting.
Officials said that 15 economic zones were currently functional across the province, while plans were under way to establish seven more.
They added that the company had so far facilitated the creation of around 107,000 employment opportunities.
Officials highlighted issues confronting various economic zones, including the Yaka Ghund Marble City, Katlang Economic Zone and other proposed industrial projects.
Governor Kundi said promotion of industries could generate thousands of employment opportunities for the people and play a vital role in ensuring sustainable economic growth. He emphasised encouraging private sector investment by providing a business-friendly environment and facilitating investors under the Ease of Doing Business Policy.
Mr Kundi directed authorities to resolve functional issues of economic zones on a priority basis and asked them to consult the Finance Department regarding land acquisition and payment-related matters for new economic zone projects and present practical proposals.
He also instructed officials to convene immediate meetings with relevant federal and provincial departments to address the issues facing economic zones, ensuring all stakeholders were taken into confidence for effective and practical solutions.
The governor said matters relating to federal departments should be taken up with the federal government for timely resolution and stressed the need to address security concerns, site selection and other administrative challenges affecting economic zones.
He said that some economic zones were located in areas facing law and order challenges. He called for a comprehensive review to devise workable solutions so that industrial activities could be initiated there.
Mr Kundi directed authorities to expedite action for resolving financial issues and legal disputes, remove all obstacles affecting the functionality of economic zones and ensure early progress on pending matters.
Published in Dawn, October 20th, 2026

title: Industry calls for easier rules as FBR urges export growth
text:
KARACHI: Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) Chief Langrial urged exporters to expand the presence of Pakistani products in international markets, as industry leaders raised concerns over complicated regulations, digital invoicing difficulties and the tax burden on already compliant businesses.
During a meeting with a delegation from the Korangi Association of Trade and Industry (Kati), led by its president, Sheikh Umer Rehan, FBR Chairman Rashid Mahmood Langrial called on exporters to make effective use of available resources to increase national exports.
He said the FBR would soon hold meetings with major exporters to review their concerns, identify obstacles to export growth and take necessary measures to address them.
The FBR chairman also said the authority was pursuing tax system digitalisation and automated mechanisms to bring non-filers into the tax net.
  Kati flags costly regulations, digital invoicing; Langrial pledges action on concerns
Mr Rehan, however, said digitalisation of the tax system was essential, but practical difficulties faced by industries during the implementation of digital invoicing needed to be resolved.
He called on the government to provide businesses with proper guidance and technical assistance and establish effective coordination mechanisms to address implementation challenges. He said tax transparency should be strengthened without disrupting industrial and commercial activities.
Mr Rehan also stressed that broadening the tax base required bringing all individuals and businesses legally liable to pay taxes into the system. The tax burden, he said, should not remain concentrated on already compliant businesses.
He called on authorities to identify untaxed sectors and ensure uniform enforcement of tax laws across all relevant segments. The Kati president also highlighted tax and duty-related issues affecting industries in the Korangi Industrial Area, particularly the ghee and edible oil sector.
He urged the government to review unnecessary statutory regulatory orders (SROs) and complicated regulatory requirements that obstruct business operations and increase production costs. Such rules, he said, should be simplified and made practical to improve the competitiveness of local industries.
Responding to the delegation’s concerns, Mr Langrial assured its members that necessary steps would be taken to resolve the issues.
Published in Dawn, October 20th, 2026

title: SECP probes discrepancies in SE Fruits IPO
text:
ISLAMABAD: The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) has launched an investigation into the initial public offering (IPO) of SE Fruits and Vegetable Limited after an anonymous complaint revealed major financial discrepancies in the company’s audit report, officials said.
The commission is also looking to strengthen the Audit Oversight Board after discrepancies were detected in the company’s audit report. The inquiry will examine whether any gaps, omissions or negligence occurred during the IPO approval process and determine responsibility where warranted.
The inquiry follows an anonymous complaint received on Sept 11, two days after the SECP approved the company’s prospectus based on its audited financial statements.
A preliminary review flagged differences between reported sales and sales tax returns for 2022-26, local sales that were not reflected in the company’s 2024 income tax return and a gap between reported sales, after accounting for closing receivables, and bank credits.
The complaint questioned the sales figures disclosed in the prospectus, which were based on the company’s audit report.
The SECP asked SE Fruits and Vegetable Ltd., its consultant to the issue and its auditors to provide documents and explain the discrepancies.
The company submitted additional material following a meeting with the parties concerned. The inquiry will examine the information and explanations provided to determine whether the differences resulted from inaccurate disclosures, accounting treatment or other factors.
The IPO process was suspended while the concerns were examined, and the company later withdrew its application.
The investigation will review the Pakistan Stock Exchange’s role as a front-line regulator, the consultant to the issue’s due diligence, its role in preparing the prospectus and certifying its accuracy, and the auditor’s examination of the company’s financial statements.
The inquiry will also assess the SECP’s internal procedures for reviewing IPO applications and handling the complaint.
Published in Dawn, October 20th, 2026

title: Govt calls on all political parties to unite, forge consensus against terrorism and set aside differences | The Express Tribune
text:
Govt calls on all political parties to unite, forge consensus against terrorism and set aside differences
Sanaullah says terrorism is a national issue, if all parties reach an agreement PM is ready to resolve it
ISLAMABAD:
The government on Tuesday urged all political parties to set aside their differences and forge a consensus on a joint strategy to combat terrorism, saying it was a national issue that required collective efforts and a unified response.
“This is a national issue. We can sit together and formulate a policy. When everyone puts their heads together, a decision can be made, as happened when Zarb-e-Azb was launched. Even now, if all political parties [..] sit together and discuss this issue, I am making an offer today: if all parties come together and reach an agreement on this issue, the prime minister is still willing to invite them to resolve it. He is ready to proceed with these operations with everyone’s support," said Special Adviser to the Prime Minister Rana Sanaullah while speaking in the Senate.
This is not the first time the government has invited the opposition for talks. The government’s offer comes amid heightened tensions following the Centre’s imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P), citing the deteriorating security situation and what it described as a lack of cooperation from the provincial administration in the fight against terrorism. Parliament has also endorsed the measures, with both houses approving the relevant proposals.
Sanaullah during today's Senate session said terrorism was a national issue that required all political parties to set aside their differences and agree on a joint strategy, adding that the government was prepared to engage with the opposition to resolve the matter.
He urged Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl leader Maulana Abdul Wasey to speak to party chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman.
Comparing the provincial governments’ approaches to counterterrorism, Sanaullah accused the K-P government of failing to provide the cooperation needed to eliminate terrorism, while saying the Balochistan government was fully cooperating with the armed forces and the federal government.
He said the now non-functional (K-P) chief minister Sohail Afridi had repeatedly stated that he would not allow operations in the province, adding that provincial apex committees provided a forum for discussing security matters, with the core commander attending meetings under the respective chief ministers’ leadership.
Sanaullah said he had attended apex committee meetings in Balochistan alongside the prime minister, where issues were discussed openly. In contrast, he said, only one meeting had taken place in K-P in 11 months, "and in that meeting the way that the CM was taken there Mohsin Naqvi described those circumstances."
“If you only raise the issue of terrorism to create headlines, I do not think that is national service or the right approach to resolving the problem,” he said.
Read: PHC seeks Centre’s response over imposition of emergency, governor’s rule in K-P
Sanaullah also criticised National Assembly opposition leader Raja Nasir Abbas for refusing to meet the prime minister or visit the speaker’s chamber, despite accepting the position of opposition leader.
Recalling an encounter with Abbas during a joint sitting of parliament, Sanaullah said, “I told him to leave this stubbornness aside and set a time to meet the prime minister,” adding that Abbas had refused, saying he did not recognise the National Assembly speaker.
Sanaullah questioned how Abbas could accept the position and its associated privileges while refusing to engage with the government through parliamentary channels.
The adviser also recalled negotiations with Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) over elections after the party dissolved its provincial assemblies. He said both sides had agreed to hold general elections in the first week of September, but the agreement subsequently fell through.
Sanaullah said PTI leader Shah Mahmood Qureshi had asked for time to inform the party’s founding chairman, Imran Khan, that the negotiating committees had reached an understanding. However, he said the party later rejected the agreement.
He added that a draft of the negotiations was available to the media and that committee members, including Sohail Afridi, had exchanged messages about the discussions.
Referring to recent negotiations, Sanaullah said several matters, including arrangements for meetings and other outstanding issues, had been settled. The parties had also discussed forming a political committee comprising representatives from both sides to address unresolved matters.
However, he said, the opposition had refused to sign the draft over one point: supporting counterterrorism operations and fulfilling its responsibilities in the fight against terrorism.
Sanaullah also responded to remarks by PTI leader Mashal Yousafzai about a helicopter and an alleged message conveyed during negotiations. He said the opposition had claimed it was asked to sign an agreement under which an emergency would be imposed within 72 hours and to call off its long march unconditionally.
Read more: 'No link between K-P emergency, minerals'
“If this was your preparation, as has now come to light, then I consider this another missed opportunity,” he said.
Sanaullah said security personnel continued to be killed in the fight against terrorism, paying tribute to an army major who was martyred yesterday in an IED attack. He criticised what he said was a narrative targeting an entire institution and its head, accusing some political actors of making derogatory remarks and amplifying them through social media.
Sanaullah said the government could restrict meetings with Imran under the law if party leaders continued to make derogatory remarks about the head of a state institution. “Then, under the rules and the law, restrictions can be imposed on meetings,” he said.
Sanaullah also questioned PTI’s repeated attempts to secure political gains through different channels, including the courts and US President Donald Trump, rather than resolving its disputes through negotiations.
He said the recent long march was PTI’s third such attempt and recalled earlier marches towards Islamabad, adding that it was PTI leaders, rather than the government, who had spoken about bringing two million people to the capital and launching an attack.
He urged the opposition to reconsider its approach and resolve its outstanding issues through dialogue, reiterating that the fight against terrorism required collective national support.
Tariq Fazal urges unity on terrorism
Later in the day, Federal Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Tariq Fazal Chaudhry urged opposition parties to engage with the government on a single-point agenda of building consensus against terrorism and formulating a joint policy to tackle the issue.
“Let us begin with this single issue and this single-point agenda — that we have to develop a consensus against terrorism. Two opposition leaders were with me at a programme yesterday, and they said that all political parties should develop a consensus against terrorism. I extended the invitation yesterday, and I am extending it again today to all opposition parties — and our allies are already with us — to come and sit together so that we can develop a consensus against terrorism," the minister said.
He urged all political parties to reach a consensus against terrorism, saying it was an issue on which “we should all be united” and that Pakistan’s peace and the future of its children were at stake.
Chaudhry said political differences should not come at the expense of national interests, asking why parties could not reach a consensus on issues concerning Pakistan’s development, prosperity and peace.
“Politics is not meant to compromise the national interest,” he said, reiterating his invitation to opposition parties to work together against terrorism.
Taking aim at the PTI’s performance in K-P, Chaudhry questioned why the party had failed to establish peace despite being in power in the province for 10 to 12 years, including its more recent two-and-a-half-year tenure.
“On one side, bombs are exploding, and the bodies of our martyred soldiers, officers, police personnel and Frontier Corps personnel are being sent to their homes. On the other, you have created a strange spectacle on the streets, as if it were an Under-19 tournament,” he said.
“Neither does the province function this way, nor does the country,” he added, urging the PTI to work with the federal government and contribute to ongoing intelligence-based operations.
“Even today, if you come to your senses and sit with the federal government, your own leaders are speaking. Develop a consensus on this issue,” he said, adding that the government remained committed to the fight against terrorism.
Chaudhry also defended the imposition of emergency in K-P, saying the federal government had taken the step in response to security challenges rather than out of a desire to assume control of the province.
He said an advisory council had been formed comprising technocrats with expertise in their respective fields, while a separate council included tribal elders to ensure local communities were consulted on intelligence-based operations.
“The federal government and the armed forces are committed to continuing operations against terrorists until terrorism is completely eliminated,” he said.
Distinguishing K-P and Balochistan, Chaudhry said the provincial administration and chief minister in Balochistan were cooperating with the federal government and law enforcement agencies in the fight against terrorism.
“The chief minister is standing shoulder to shoulder with our law enforcement agencies and is on the front line in confronting terrorists,” he said, adding that the Balochistan government was not refusing to cooperate with counterterrorism operations.
The minister also criticised those linking the imposition of emergency to the province’s mineral resources, arguing that Pakistan needed to utilise its natural wealth to generate resources for development and reduce its debt burden.
“If Allah has blessed Pakistan with these treasures, which have remained buried for 80 years, and you want to keep them buried for another 80 or 180 years, that is your choice,” he said.
He maintained that the people of the province where minerals were located would have the first right to those resources. He added that international companies involved in exploration would be expected to follow international standards and ensure their activities did not create difficulties for local communities.
Resources generated through minerals, oil and gas, he said, could help fund improvements in education and healthcare across the country.
He said the federal government’s two primary objectives were to establish lasting peace and completely eliminate terrorism, adding that emergency would remain in place until those targets were achieved.
“We can compromise on politics, but we cannot compromise on the state, the interests of the state or state institutions,” he said.
Calls for dialogue
The government and opposition made several attempts to reach a political understanding before emergency and governor’s rule were imposed in K-P.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif made multiple offers of talks to PTI, saying the government was prepared to engage with the opposition if the party ended its long march and sit-ins.
PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari also urged the federal government to pursue dialogue before resorting to constitutional measures, saying political parties needed to work together against terrorism. He later offered to approach PM Shehbaz to end the emergency if the opposition agreed to political dialogue.
Talks between the government and opposition subsequently broke down amid disagreements over access to PTI founder Imran Khan and the provincial government’s role in counterterrorism. The government said the parties had agreed on most points but could not reach consensus on support for counterterrorism operations. PTI, however, blamed the government’s refusal to meet its demands, particularly access to Khan, for the deadlock.
After negotiations failed, the federal government imposed emergency and governor’s rule in K-P on October 11, citing the deteriorating security situation and what it said was a lack of cooperation from the provincial administration in the fight against terrorism. PM Shehbaz said the government had been left with no option but to take the measures after efforts to reach an agreement failed. The move brought the PTI-led provincial administration to an end and prompted legal challenges.
