The nation must turn its grief into action so that no mother ever again sends her child to school with a loving kiss in the morning, only to receive a lifeless body in return.

title: Lack of cricket grounds spurs new trend of tournaments on agricultural land
text:
Muhammad Aatif Ismail Multan, Oct 18 (APP):For a few weeks each year, ordinary agricultural fields in the villages of South Punjab undergo a remarkable transformation. The land that usually waits for the next crop becomes a cricketing arena, where makeshift pitches are prepared, boundaries are marked and young players gather with dreams far bigger than the fields on which they play. In villages where proper cricket grounds remain scarce, temporarily …
Lack of cricket grounds spurs new trend of tournaments on agricultural land
Muhammad Aatif Ismail
Multan, Oct 18 (APP):For a few weeks each year, ordinary agricultural fields in the villages of South Punjab undergo a remarkable transformation. The land that usually waits for the next crop becomes a cricketing arena, where makeshift pitches are prepared, boundaries are marked and young players gather with dreams far bigger than the fields on which they
play.
In villages where proper cricket grounds remain scarce, temporarily vacant farmland has become an unlikely home for the sport.
With permission from farmers and landowners, young enthusiasts transform agricultural plots into makeshift grounds, organize local tournaments and invite teams from neighboring villages.
When the competitions end, the wickets are dismantled, the crowds disperse and the land returns to its agricultural purpose.
Yet, beneath this inspiring display of community spirit lies a troubling reality: a shortage of sports infrastructure continues to force rural youngsters to borrow fields simply to pursue their passion for cricket.
“There are no proper cricket grounds in our village, which creates serious difficulties for us and prevents local talent from emerging,” said Rana Muhammad Arif, a cricketer from Chak 232-EB, Vehari.
He added that young players in many parts of South Punjab faced similar challenges.
His concern echoes the frustration of countless aspiring cricketers whose ambitions often collide with the absence of basic playing facilities. In villages where suitable grounds are unavailable, even regular practice becomes a challenge, leaving talented youngsters with limited opportunities to sharpen their skills, compete at higher levels and earn
recognition.
Muhammad Dilawar, a resident of Basti Nau, Multan, said village youngsters had found a practical way to keep their sporting dreams alive. They approach farmers, landowners and influential community members to seek temporary permission to use vacant agricultural land.
With their cooperation, they prepare pitches, mark boundaries and arrange tournaments that generally last 15 to 20 days, sometimes extending beyond a month.
What begins as a makeshift arrangement often grows into a celebration of village life. Teams arrive from surrounding settlements, spectators gather along the boundaries, and the sound of bat striking ball brings the fields alive.
For a brief period, these otherwise quiet stretches of farmland become centers of excitement, rivalry and collective
pride.
Dilawar said such competitions gave young players an opportunity to display their abilities, test themselves against unfamiliar opponents and experience organized cricket without travelling long distances in search of suitable grounds.
Muhammad Naveed, another cricket enthusiast, said community cooperation had become essential to sustaining the game in areas lacking permanent facilities. Village elders, nambardars and influential landowners often helped by making land available until farming activities resumed.
Similar tournaments have recently been held in Chak 31 of Vehari district, while competitions in Chak 69 of Mailsi tehsil have become a regular annual feature, according to Muhammad Ramzan, a coach and sponsor of a local cricket club.
These events demonstrate how rural communities are mobilizing their limited resources to keep cricket alive despite the absence of dedicated playing fields.
Tennis-ball cricket has further strengthened the popularity of these tournaments. Its relatively low cost and flexible arrangements allow youngsters from different economic backgrounds to participate without the expense associated with more formal competitions.
Local businesses and individual sponsors frequently contribute towards equipment, prizes and other tournament expenses. Overseas Pakistanis who retain close ties with their hometowns also play an important role in supporting these activities, helping village competitions continue despite limited financial resources.
Beyond the boundaries, however, the tournaments offer something even more valuable than sporting entertainment. They bring communities together, encourage teamwork and healthy competition, and give youngsters a constructive outlet for their energy.
Representing one’s village before an enthusiastic crowd can build confidence, strengthen friendships and inspire players to pursue the game more seriously.
But when the final ball is bowled and the temporary wickets are pulled apart, an uncomfortable question remains: why should young cricketers in a region so passionate about the game have to depend on borrowed agricultural land to play it?.
Temporary grounds may provide an immediate solution, but they cannot replace permanent facilities that remain accessible throughout the year. Without reliable playing surfaces, aspiring cricketers struggle to practice consistently, improve their performance and participate in structured competitions.
Their talent may be visible to an entire village, yet remain beyond the reach of coaches, talent scouts and formal cricket pathways.
The responsibility now rests with the government and local administrations to turn this grassroots enthusiasm into a lasting sporting opportunity. Suitable public land could be identified for village-level cricket grounds, with basic facilities developed in consultation with local communities.
Schools, sports departments, local governments and private sponsors could work together to establish affordable playing spaces.
Transparent partnerships could also encourage overseas Pakistanis and local philanthropists to invest in village sports projects. Even modest improvements to playing surfaces and basic facilities could benefit generations of youngsters, replacing temporary arrangements with permanent opportunities.
For now, the cricket grounds of South Punjab remain temporary creations carved out of agricultural land. When the tournaments end, spectators return home, the wickets disappear and farmers prepare their fields for the next crop. The cheers fade, the boundaries vanish and the game gives way to the demands of the soil.
But the dreams born on those fields do not disappear with the last match.
Behind every makeshift pitch stands a generation of young players waiting for a fair chance to prove itself. Providing permanent cricket grounds would mean more than laying a pitch or marking a boundary.
It would mean recognizing rural talent, investing in young people and ensuring that a shortage of facilities does not decide the limits of their ambitions.
South Punjab’s youngsters have already shown that passion can turn farmland into a sporting arena. The challenge now is for the authorities to ensure that their dreams no longer have to depend on the next vacant field.

title: From a mother’s bridal trunk to rental racks: a tradition in transition
text:
Moniba Iftikhar ISLAMABAD, Oct 18 (APP):Once, a daughter’s wedding began taking shape in her mother’s hands long before the celebrations arrived. Gold earrings were purchased after months of saving, embroidered dresses were carefully folded and a bridal trunk slowly filled with garments intended for the most memorable days of a young woman’s life. Each possession reflected a mother’s affection, sacrifice and hope for her daughter’s future. Today, that familiar scene …
From a mother’s bridal trunk to rental racks: a tradition in transition
Moniba Iftikhar
ISLAMABAD, Oct 18 (APP):Once, a daughter’s wedding began taking shape in her mother’s hands long before the celebrations arrived. Gold earrings were purchased after months of saving, embroidered dresses were carefully folded and a bridal trunk slowly filled with garments intended for the most memorable days of a young woman’s life.
Each possession reflected a mother’s affection, sacrifice and hope for her daughter’s future.
Today, that familiar scene is changing.
        A generation influenced by social media, celebrity weddings and evolving fashion trends is discovering new ways to prepare for marriage.
       Rental boutiques, artificial jewellery and online resale platforms are increasingly becoming part of bridal shopping, transforming how families preserve traditions passed down through generations.
         For many Pakistani households, preparing a bridal trousseau was once an essential family ritual. Mothers selected outfits for wedding ceremonies, musical celebrations and family gatherings, often preserving expensive garments and jewellery as heirlooms.
         The collection represented not merely material possessions but years of planning, sacrifice and emotional investment.
          However, rising gold prices and the growing cost of designer clothing are encouraging families to reconsider how these customs can be maintained.
         In Islamabad, gold remains a symbol of family honor, affection and financial security. With 24-karat gold trading at around Rs. 432,500 per tola, according to the rate cited for this report, purchasing a traditional bridal jewellery set has become a substantial expense for middle-class households.
            Usman, a jeweller at Islamabad’s Super Market, told APP that a conventional bridal gold set can cost well over Rs. 1.5 million, depending on its weight and design. For parents who traditionally regarded gold as an essential wedding gift, the expense is prompting a reassessment of long-established expectations.
        Artificial jewellery offers an alternative, but even imitation ornaments can cost tens of thousands of rupees. Elaborate sets featuring imported stones, zircon embellishments, intricate glasswork and gold plating have become popular among brides seeking traditional grandeur without investing in precious metals.
            In Rawalpindi’ s Saddar commercial area, Muhammad Imran, who manages a jewellery kiosk, says improvements in artificial jewellery craftsmanship have expanded the choices available to brides.
         Designs inspired by Turkish fashion and traditional bridal ornaments allow young women to achieve an elaborate appearance without purchasing genuine gold.
        According to Imran, artificial jewellery sets cost between Rs. 15,000 and Rs. 50,000 to purchase, depending on their design and quality. Renting offers another option for brides who want different ornaments to complement multiple wedding outfits.
         Social media is adding another dimension to this transformation. Celebrity weddings, fashion influencers and bloggers regularly showcase elaborate bridal ensembles, statement jewellery and designer collections on Instagram, TikTok and YouTube.
       Their wedding photographs and styling videos have become sources of inspiration for young women planning their own celebrations.
        However, recreating celebrity-inspired looks does not always mean purchasing expensive designer pieces. Many brides now explore rental boutiques, artificial jewellery and online resale platforms to achieve similar styles at a fraction of the retail cost.
       The trend reflects a generation that values fashionable appearances and memorable photographs while becoming more conscious of the expense involved.
              The shift is particularly visible in bridal clothing, where the tradition of purchasing multiple outfits is increasingly giving way to rental arrangements.
                Urwa Shahid faced this dilemma before her winter wedding. Like many brides, she dreamed of wearing an elaborate designer outfit on her special day. However, the cost of purchasing her preferred dress made her reconsider the traditional approach.
          Following a friend’s recommendation, she explored Rawalpindi’ s rental markets and found an outfit that matched her vision without requiring the full purchase price. Her experience illustrates how young brides are treating rental arrangements as a practical choice rather than a compromise.
           At Rabi Center on Murree Road in Rawalpindi, boutique proprietor Tariq Mahmood told APP that brides increasingly seek designer-style clothing through rental arrangements.
           According to Amir, bridal ensembles that cost between Rs. 200,000 and Rs. 600,000 to purchase may be available for rent for approximately Rs. 20,000 to Rs. 60,000, depending on their design and rental terms.
           For families preparing for several wedding functions, the savings can be considerable. Instead of purchasing a separate expensive outfit for every occasion, brides can rent different ensembles and reserve their money for household needs and future plans.
              Zainab, a bride-to-be browsing outfits at Rabi Center, believes spending Rs. 400,000 to Rs. 500,000 on a dress worn for only a few hours is difficult to justify when the same amount could contribute towards establishing a new household.
             As the wedding season gathers pace, jewellery shops are witnessing a steady stream of mothers and daughters searching for ways to add sparkle to their bridal and wedding attire without stretching their household budgets. With the rising cost of living making traditional wedding purchases increasingly difficult, renting jewellery is emerging as a practical alternative for many families.
             Kashif, a jewellery seller from Rawalpindi, said his business also reaches customers through TikTok, where they can browse designs and explore available options online. His jewellery sets start at Rs15,000, while rental options range from Rs10,000 to Rs12,000.
             Although he would prefer customers to purchase jewellery rather than rent it, Kashif acknowledged that rising costs are changing consumer preferences. For many families, renting offers a way to achieve the desired wedding look without the financial burden of buying expensive sets that may be worn only on special occasions.
          Meanwhile, Asia, who is helping prepare for her sister’s wedding, says recommendations from friends have encouraged her family to explore rental boutiques.
            Online marketplaces also allow young women to discover rental services, compare designs and find buyers for bridal dresses after their weddings.
           Despite these changes, the emotional significance of the bridal trousseau remains. For mothers who spent years assembling their daughters’ wedding possessions, moving away from permanent ownership may feel like the loss of a cherished ritual. Yet the meaning of their efforts need not disappear with the bridal trunk.
             A daughter can still wear her mother’s necklace, preserve an inherited ornament or carry a family heirloom alongside a rented designer dress.
                     Such choices allow traditional values and contemporary fashion to coexist.
            From Islamabad’s jewellery counters to Rawalpindi’ s rental boutiques and online marketplaces, Pakistan’s bridal culture is finding new expressions.
          The modern bride may choose a rented lehenga over an expensive purchase or artificial jewellery over genuine gold, but the desire to celebrate a daughter’s new beginning remains unchanged.
          As bridal trunks make room for rental racks and digital shopping, the tradition continues to evolve, shaped by a generation seeking both fashionable celebrations and financial independence.

title: Collective resolve, lasting peace: addressing KP’s security challenge
text:
Political unity, institutional coordination and a comprehensive strategy are essential for combating terrorism and ensuring sustainable, lasting peace and development in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP), experts said.
Collective resolve, lasting peace: addressing KP’s security challenge
Fakhar-e-Alam
PESHAWAR, Oct 11 (APP):Political unity, institutional coordination and a comprehensive strategy are essential for combating terrorism and ensuring sustainable, lasting peace and development in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP), experts said.
      They stressed that the security challenges facing the province required close cooperation between the federal and provincial governments, police, security, intelligence agencies and civil society to protect citizens and strengthen public confidence.
      MPA Malik Tariq Awan said combating terrorism should remain a shared priority beyond political differences.
“The issue between the state and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is not politics but combating terrorism,” he said, emphasizing
that political activities and public gatherings could continue alongside collective efforts to maintain peace and
security.
      Talking to APP, he said around 6,200 terrorism-related incidents had occurred in KP over the past two years, claiming nearly 1,200 lives. He also claimed that 37 suicide attacks had involved Afghan nationals, including 14 during the current year. These figures require verification from official records.
      Tariq Awan highlighted the importance of strengthening the provincial Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) through improved human resources, training and operational capacity.
            He also acknowledged the sacrifices of the army, police and other security institutions in combating
militancy.
      Former Inspector General of Police Syed Akhtar Ali Shah said counter-terrorism required effective policing, intelligence coordination, prosecution, community engagement and sustained institutional support.
      He said Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and the provincial government had an important role in addressing public concerns, protecting fundamental rights and cooperating with federal authorities to prevent terrorist
violence.
      Shah emphasized that insecurity affected education, business, tourism, investment and everyday life, making a coordinated response essential for restoring public confidence and supporting economic growth.
      He called for a clearly defined counter-terrorism framework supported by practical measures, institutional coordination and regular communication with citizens.
         “Effective security policy depends heavily on coordination among federal and provincial governments and state institutions rather than isolated political positions,” he said, stressing that cooperation was necessary for lasting
peace.
          Professor Dr Zahid Anwar of the Department of Political Science at the University of Peshawar said statements by political leaders in a terrorism-affected province carried considerable weight and could influence public confidence and relations among institutions.
          He said political differences were normal in a democracy, but security required a shared commitment to protecting citizens and strengthening institutional cooperation.
          Referring to the chief minister’s reported statement about eradicating terrorism within a month, the discussion highlighted the importance of translating public commitments into practical measures, clear objectives and sustained action.
            Anwar said peace was essential for development, investment and tourism, adding that businesses needed predictable conditions and families required safe communities.
             Lawyer Noman Bukhari said counter-terrorism efforts should combine security measures with socioeconomic development. Decades of terrorism had deeply affected KP, from the Army Public School tragedy to insecurity in the merged tribal districts.
            He acknowledged the gains achieved through military operations and intelligence efforts, while emphasizing the importance of addressing the social and economic conditions that extremist groups could exploit.
Bukhari identified unemployment, educational disparities, economic inequality and social exclusion as challenges requiring sustained attention.
       He said access to quality education, employment and essential services could help communities resist extremist recruitment.
          He called for educational reforms, improved healthcare, equal opportunities and better public services, particularly for under served communities. He also stressed that educational institutions, including seminaries, should promote tolerance, critical thinking and peaceful coexistence.
           Professor Dr Jamil Khan, Director of the Centre for Conflict Studies at the University of Peshawar, said balanced regional development was important for sustainable peace.
          He highlighted the need to improve education, employment and infrastructure in remote areas, particularly southern KP and the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas.
            “The answer lies in giving these areas priority in development and education,” he said, emphasizing that better public services and economic opportunities could strengthen trust between communities and state
institutions.
            Khan added that development projects and educational reforms could provide young people with constructive alternatives to extremist ideologies while strengthening social cohesion.
             According to Ministry of Finance documents, the federal government transferred Rs2,347 billion to KP under the National Finance Commission (NFC) Award during fiscal years 2024-25 and 2025-26, including Rs1,103 billion and Rs1,244 billion, respectively.
            Under the existing NFC arrangement, KP also receives an additional one per cent of the divisible pool for expenditures related to the war against terrorism.
             Ministry of Finance officials said 57.5 per cent of the Federal Board of Revenue’s tax collection was distributed among provinces under the NFC formula, while 42.5 per cent remained with the federal government.
          Experts emphasized that effective utilization of available resources could strengthen police capacity, improve public services and support development in vulnerable areas.
          They called for a comprehensive strategy combining security operations, institutional cooperation, education, employment and community engagement. They also stressed that political dialogue should support a common approach to counter-terrorism.
            The experts welcomed Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s reported offer of dialogue as an important opportunity to strengthen federal-provincial cooperation, urging Chief Minister Sohail Afridi to engage constructively with the initiative to develop a unified strategy for combating terrorism and ensuring lasting peace, stability and prosperity in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
             They said the success of counter-terrorism efforts would ultimately be measured not merely by operations on the ground, but by safer communities, thriving schools, flourishing businesses and the freedom of citizens to live and work without fear, paving the way for a future defined by peace, prosperity and renewed hope.

title: Pakhiwas: The wandering families who call the boundless open sky their home
text:
Across the plains of South Punjab, families known as “Pakhiwas” live in small tents on vacant pieces of land. They stay in one place for some time before moving elsewhere, carrying their belongings, traditional skills and memories of the places they have visited. For them, life is a journey and a temporary shelter is home.
Pakhiwas: The wandering families who call the boundless open sky their home
Muhammad Atif Ismail
MULTAN, Oct 11 (APP):Across the plains of South Punjab, families known as “Pakhiwas” live in small tents on vacant pieces of land. They stay in one place for some time before moving elsewhere, carrying their belongings, traditional skills and memories of the places they have visited. For them, life is a journey and a temporary shelter is home.
        The word “Pakhi” means bird in the local language. Like birds that wander from place to place, these families travel in search of work and shelter, with the open sky as their constant companion.
        Their way of life differs from that of settled communities, yet they have preserved their traditions, ancestral occupations and cultural identity across generations.
For Pakhiwas families, home is not always a house with walls and a roof.
       Sometimes, it is a tent beneath a tree, a patch of open ground, or a shelter built from whatever materials are available.Their lives remain closely linked to nature, changing seasons and the daily struggle to earn a living.
Saleem Pakhiwas says he has spent his entire life living this way.
        “Since I opened my eyes, I have seen our families moving from one place to another and putting up tents wherever we find a suitable place,” he says.
        Saleem makes different kinds of baskets to earn a living. His work requires patience and skill, and his products serve practical purposes in everyday life. As factory-made goods become increasingly common, his craft represents a traditional livelihood that continues to survive in the region.
        Other community members pursue different occupations. Some collect wastepaper and scrap to support their families. Their work also helps recover materials for reuse and recycling, although their contribution often goes
unnoticed.
Akram Pakhiwas, who has spent much of his life in different parts of Multan, earns money by collecting mango stones.
           He gathers them and sells them to farmers and nursery owners who use them to grow mango plants.
South Punjab is famous for its mango orchards, and Akram has connected his livelihood with the region’s agricultural economy.
          What many people discard after eating a mango becomes a source of income for him and a useful resource for nursery growers. His work demonstrates how people with limited resources find opportunities in things others leave
behind.
          Life in a tent may seem difficult to those accustomed to permanent homes, but Pakhiwas families have learned to adapt. Akram acknowledges that they lack many facilities available to settled households, yet years of experience have taught them to manage everyday challenges.
         Summer heat in Multan can be particularly harsh for people living in temporary shelters. Akram says families use small solar panels to meet some basic electricity needs, making daily life more manageable. This reflects how communities with limited resources are finding ways to benefit from modern technology.
           Winter brings different challenges. Families cover their shelters carefully to protect themselves from cold winds, using materials and methods learned over generations. Although their homes are simple, experience helps them adapt to changing weather.
           Healthcare remains a concern. Akram says families generally obtain medicines from local hakims. Access to regular medical check-ups and nearby health facilities can be difficult when they frequently change locations.
        Children spend much of their time playing outdoors, often in the soil around their tents. Their surroundings become their playground, bringing them into close contact with nature.
          However, clean drinking water, proper nutrition, vaccination, and timely medical care remain essential for their healthy development.
          Education presents another major challenge. Many children from mobile families struggle to attend school regularly because frequent relocation makes it difficult to maintain contact with a single school. Consequently, they may miss opportunities to develop reading, writing, and other essential skills.
            Akram says the community has no land of its own, while many members also lack national identity cards. Without these documents, accessing public services and completing official procedures can become difficult.
        Despite these challenges, Pakhiwas families continue to preserve traditions passed down by their elders. They learn their occupations through observation and practice, whether making baskets, collecting scrap, or gathering mango stones. These skills form part of South Punjab’s cultural heritage, although they rarely receive wider recognition.
             Their story is not only about hardship. It is also about hard work, adaptability, and the determination to survive with limited means. They make use of available resources, find work in different places, and carry their household lives wherever circumstances take them.
           At the same time, respecting their culture must go hand in hand with better access to education, healthcare, clean water, and identity documents. Mobile health services, flexible schooling arrangements and assistance with registration could help improve their lives without forcing them to abandon their traditional way of living.
             As evening falls over the plains of South Punjab, Pakhiwas families return to their tents after a day of work. Children play nearby, elders share experiences and preparations begin for another night beneath the open
sky.
         Their homes may have no permanent address, but their lives hold generations of traditions, timeless skills and stories of resilience. Like birds soaring across the endless skies of South Punjab, the Pakhiwas continue their journey through life, carrying the weight of their struggles, the legacy of their ancestors and an unbroken hope for a brighter tomorrow.

title: Before the classroom door: Lost schoolbags, packed private vans and children at risk
text:
Every morning, private school vans move through Islamabad and Rawalpindi carrying children to their educational institutions. For parents, the journey is part of the daily routine, but for some children, the short trip to school can bring risks that often go unnoticed.
Before the classroom door: Lost schoolbags, packed private vans and children at risk
Moniba Iftikhar
ISLAMABAD, Oct 11 (APP):Every morning, private school vans move through Islamabad and Rawalpindi carrying children to their educational institutions. For parents, the journey is part of the daily routine, but for some children, the short trip to school can bring risks that often go unnoticed.
        Behind the doors of some vans, children are packed into limited space, schoolbags are placed between seats or hung outside the vehicle and drivers hurry through busy roads to complete their routes on time.
       For Class 6 student Yumna, the concern became clear when she reached school one morning without her
schoolbag. The bag had reportedly fallen from the private van somewhere along the route.
        Her books, notebooks and homework were gone, while neither the driver nor other passengers noticed the
incident.
        Teacher Fouzia of F-10/2 Model Girls College noticed Yumna Amin without her schoolbag and immediately contacted her mother, asking her to speak to the driver and find out where the bag had been lost.
       The belongings could be replaced, but the incident raised a more serious question: if a schoolbag could fall from a moving vehicle without anyone noticing, how closely were the children being watched?
        Yumna also complained about the limited space inside school vans, saying children often have to share insufficient room with their schoolbags.
          She also raised concerns about drivers rushing through traffic, leaving young passengers exposed to risks beyond their control.
         For many families, however, private school transport is not a choice but a necessity. Parents leave for work early, while professional and household responsibilities make it difficult to manage school timings themselves. Vans, buses and rickshaws therefore remain an important means of transport for schoolchildren.
        Mrs Nayab Ali said repeated encounters with what she described as irresponsible behaviour by school-van drivers eventually led her to arrange the pick-and-drop of her own children.
       She said many parents could not make the same arrangement because of work and family commitments and therefore had to depend on school transport.
     She stressed that such dependence should not become blind trust and that people entrusted with children must be properly verified and held accountable.
      Another parent Arsalan Rao said he had repeatedly seen school pick-and-drop drivers violating traffic
rules.
       “Countless times, I have seen van drivers flout traffic rules, yet traffic police often appear to do little to check such deplorable behaviour,” he said.
      He said reckless driving was particularly serious when children were travelling inside the vehicle, as a speeding driver was putting the lives of all passengers at risk.
        Speaking to APP, Rawalpindi traffic official Lehar Mirza said strict measures were being taken against school-van operators violating traffic and safety regulations, particularly those carrying children beyond the designated seating capacity.
             She said a special drive had also been launched against the unsafe practice of allowing schoolbags to hang from the rear or sides of moving vans, warning that such practices could endanger children as well as other road
users.
          “We are taking strict action against vehicles carrying children beyond their designated capacity and against drivers violating prescribed safety rules,” she said, adding that violators were being warned and fined.
       Lehar Mirza said the issue was not simply about traffic violations but directly concerned the safety and lives of schoolchildren. A school van, she stressed, was carrying children whose safety could not be compromised merely to accommodate additional passengers.
      She said vehicles designed for a limited number of children must not be overloaded, as overcrowding leaves children without proper seating and makes it difficult for them to move or protect themselves during sudden braking, collisions or other emergencies.
      She also warned against hanging schoolbags outside vans, saying bags could fall onto roads, create hazards for other motorists and pedestrians, or become lost without the children or driver noticing.
         Lehar Mirza said traffic officials in Rawalpindi with the directives of Senior Chief Traffic officer Farhan were carrying out checks and would continue enforcement against violators, with warnings and fines being issued where necessary.
      She said the special drive was expected to produce better results in the coming days as monitoring was being strengthened.
      Alongside enforcement, she said awareness sessions were being conducted in schools to educate students, parents, drivers and school administrations about road safety and responsible school transport.
        She urged parents to cooperate with authorities and avoid sending their children in overcrowded or unsafe vans.
       “Parents also have a responsibility. If a van is overcrowded, unsafe or the driver repeatedly violates traffic rules, the matter should be reported rather than accepted as part of the daily routine,” she said.
          Speaking to APP, Inspector Traffic Rana Ishtiaq Ahmed of the Education Wing of Islamabad Traffic Police said the department had intensified its road-safety campaign around government and private schools in and around the
Capital.
               He said police personnel had been deployed near various private schools, while awareness activities were being conducted for students, teachers, parents, drivers and school administrations.
          Rana Ishtiaq Ahmed said traffic discipline was not limited to avoiding fines. Pedestrians, particularly children, should be given the right of way at zebra crossings.
            He said traffic police encounter around 60 to 80 violators daily, including school-van drivers involved in pick-and-drop services. Depending on the offense, fines ranging from Rs500 to Rs1,500 are imposed, while vehicles failing to meet safety requirements may also face action.
             He identified overcrowding as one of the major concerns, saying vehicles designed to carry around 10 children were sometimes found carrying 18 to 20.
         Ishtiaq Ahmad also said a strict crackdown was being launched against private pick-ups and vans fitted with rear grills or metal frames used for hanging schoolbags, as such modifications could pose safety risks to children.
       He urged parents not to compromise their children’ s safety merely to save money and stressed that drivers must be properly trained and licensed.
          Taqi Jawad, Public Relations Officer and official spokesperson for Islamabad Capital Territory Police, said traffic personnel were also warning school-van drivers against over speeding, dangerous manoeuvring, illegal parking, overloading and other violations.
           An official of an authorised online school transport service operating in Islamabad and Rawalpindi said safer school transport could be provided through CNIC verification, background checks and police verification of drivers. The service provides parents with real-time journey updates, fixed pick-up and drop-off schedules, controlled passenger numbers and emergency communication.
            These measures provide a useful standard for responsible school transport: verified drivers, roadworthy vehicles, proper seating, controlled passenger numbers and communication with parents.
          Parents, meanwhile, can ask basic questions before entrusting their children to any vehicle: Who is driving? Is the driver properly licensed and verified? How many children are travelling? Does every child have a seat? Is the vehicle maintained? Are schoolbags secure?
           Yumna’ s schoolbag can be replaced. Her books can be bought again and her homework rewritten.
       But the incident offers a simple reminder that the journey to school deserves the same attention to safety as the classroom itself.
       The school run is a daily responsibility shared by parents, drivers, schools, transport providers and authorities. Each has a role in ensuring that children reach school and return home safely.
            Education begins with reaching the classroom safely. For every child travelling to school each morning, that journey should be secure, orderly and worthy of the trust placed in the adults responsible for it.
               A bag may be lost and replaced, but a child can never be replaced.

title: Kashmir Chowk: Islamabad’s fast-track infrastructure drive enters a one-month race
text:
Abdul Samad Tariq ISLAMABAD, Oct 7 (APP):Every morning, thousands of motorists travel from Rawalpindi towards Islamabad, making Kashmir Chowk a vital link in the daily movement between the twin cities. As traffic from different directions converges at the junction, the growing volume of vehicles highlights the need for modern infrastructure capable of ensuring smoother, safer and more efficient mobility. At Kashmir …
Kashmir Chowk: Islamabad’s fast-track infrastructure drive enters a one-month race
Abdul Samad Tariq
ISLAMABAD, Oct 7 (APP):Every morning, thousands of motorists travel from Rawalpindi towards Islamabad, making Kashmir Chowk a vital link in the daily movement between the twin cities.
            As traffic from different directions converges at the junction, the growing volume of vehicles highlights the need for modern infrastructure capable of ensuring smoother, safer and more efficient mobility.
      At Kashmir Chowk, traffic arriving from Islamabad, Rawalpindi and the Murree side converges, turning an already busy junction into one of the capital’s most demanding traffic points. For commuters, the familiar scene is one of long queues, frequent stoppages and precious minutes lost during peak hours.
         Now, a major infrastructure intervention is set to change that experience.
          The Rs1.4 billion Kashmir Chowk underpass, being developed by the Capital Development Authority (CDA) is designed to separate major traffic movements and provide a faster, more efficient route for thousands of motorists using the junction every day.
 According to the CDA, around 107,000 vehicles pass through Kashmir Chowk daily. With traffic volumes continuing to rise across the Islamabad-Rawalpindi metropolitan area, the need for a permanent solution has become increasingly clear.
            For commuters like Sara, a university student who travels daily from Rawalpindi towards Serena, the project is not simply another road scheme it is a long-awaited relief.
           “As someone who drives through Kashmir Chowk every day, I feel this underpass is long overdue. The congestion during peak hours is unbearable. If it is completed within the promised one-month time-frame, it will save commuters a great deal of time and stress,” she said, while stressing the importance of properly managing traffic diversions during construction.
              Rizwan, another regular motorist, also welcomed the project.
          “Thousands of vehicles pass through this junction every day, and it has become particularly difficult when traffic from the Murree side mixes with Rawalpindi-bound traffic. Separating the Rawalpindi-bound movement through the underpass is a smart solution,” he said.
           The project has gained particular attention because of the government’s decision to pursue an accelerated construction schedule.
              Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif laid the foundation stone of the underpass, which is being executed by Habib Construction Services (HCS). While the bidding documents provide a completion period of 90 days, CDA officials have said the contractor has the capacity and experience to complete the scheme in just one month.
            That ambitious target places Kashmir Chowk among the government’s fast-track infrastructure initiatives aimed at delivering visible improvements to Islamabad’s road network within a short period.
         The road arrangement planned for the junction is straightforward but significant. Traffic travelling from the Serena side towards Rawalpindi will pass through the underpass, while traffic heading towards Murree will move over it.
          Four slip roads are also part of the scheme, while approximately five acres are being incorporated for expanded road infrastructure and related facilities.
         The project’s cost has also been brought down through cost optimization. According to the CDA, the initial estimated cost of Rs1.6 billion was reduced to around Rs1.4 billion. HCS submitted a bid of Rs1.45 billion against the Rs1.486 billion amount mentioned in the Notice Inviting Tender, after another bidder was declared technically
non-responsive.
            For the government, the project therefore represents more than a new underpass. It combines cost efficiency, faster execution, engineering standards and improved mobility at one of Islamabad’s busiest junctions.
              Preparatory work, including site clearing, traffic-diversion planning and utility shifting, has already been undertaken. These steps are particularly important because construction at Kashmir Chowk must continue alongside regular traffic and existing utility infrastructure.
            CDA Chairman Sohail Ashraf has also personally reviewed the project and temporary traffic arrangements. During a September visit to the site, he directed officials to ensure effective traffic management throughout construction and called for close coordination among relevant departments.
               The message is clear: speed of construction cannot come at the expense of public convenience or safety.
             A CDA spokesperson said the project remained a priority under the authority’s fast-track development
programme.
          “With preparatory work already completed and Habib Construction Services mobilized, we are confident of delivering the project within the accelerated one-month target while maintaining quality and safety standards,” the spokesperson said. “Effective traffic management during construction remains our top priority so that the public faces minimum disruption.”
           The Kashmir Chowk project is part of a much wider transformation taking place across Islamabad.
         The CDA says it completed 18 development schemes in 2025 at a combined cost of around Rs15 billion. These included major road projects such as the Serena Interchange, Murree Road underpass, F-8 Interchange, T-Chowk flyover and Shaheen Chowk underpass, along with Park Road and the Business Facilitation Centre.
          Shaheen Chowk, completed on an accelerated basis and opened to traffic at the beginning of 2026, provides a recent example of the fast-track approach now being applied to Kashmir Chowk.
         The broader objective is to build a road network that reflects the changing mobility needs of the capital rather than simply addressing individual congestion points.
         This is increasingly important as Islamabad and Rawalpindi function as one interconnected metropolitan area. Every day, students, office workers, traders, professionals and families cross between the two cities, making efficient road links essential to economic and social activity.
The Kashmir Chowk underpass is also being developed alongside the expansion and rehabilitation of the Islamabad Expressway service road and other major connectivity projects.
            Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has said that after completion of the Kashmir Chowk underpass and Expressway expansion, travel time between Islamabad and Rawalpindi could fall to around 16 to 18 minutes.
        The projected improvement reflects the combined impact of several infrastructure projects, but Kashmir Chowk is expected to play an important role by removing a major bottleneck from the network.
          For commuters, however, the ultimate test will be simple: less waiting, smoother movement and more predictable journeys.
         For the government and CDA, the project offers another test whether modern planning, cost optimization, coordinated execution and fast-track construction can deliver infrastructure at the pace demanded by a rapidly growing capital.
        If the one-month target is achieved while maintaining safety and engineering standards, Kashmir Chowk could become more than an underpass. It could stand as another example of Islamabad’s transition towards a modern, integrated and mobility-focused urban network.
           And for the thousands of motorists who pass through the junction every day, the reward may be even simpler: fewer queues, shorter journeys and one less traffic headache on the daily route between Rawalpindi, Islamabad and the Murree side.

title: Islamabad’s renewed plastic-free push puts everyday habits under scrutiny
text:
A plastic bag picked up after a shopping trip may seem harmless, but thousands of such choices are adding to Islamabad’s growing waste problem. The renewed “Plastic-Free Islamabad” campaign is seeking to raise awareness about the environmental impact of single-use plastics and encourage residents and businesses to adopt reusable and environmentally friendly alternatives.
Islamabad’s renewed plastic-free push puts everyday habits under scrutiny
Abdul Samad Tariq
ISLAMABAD, Oct 5 (APP):A plastic bag picked up after a shopping trip may seem harmless, but thousands of such choices are adding to Islamabad’s growing waste problem. The renewed “Plastic-Free Islamabad” campaign is seeking to raise awareness about the environmental impact of single-use plastics and encourage residents and businesses to adopt reusable and environmentally friendly alternatives.
The Capital Development Authority (CDA) and Islamabad administration have launched the “Plastic-Free Islamabad” initiative on the directions of Interior Minister Syed Mohsin Raza Naqvi and CDA Chairman and Chief Commissioner Islamabad Sohail Ashraf.
  The campaign, being supervised by Additional Deputy Commissioner (General) Dr Anam Fatima, will focus on markets, commercial areas, food outlets, educational institutions, parks, recreational sites and other public places. Assistant commissioners have been tasked with monitoring activities in their respective areas.
        While the authorities are seeking greater public cooperation, the initiative also highlights a practical challenge: reducing plastic use requires changes not only in consumer behaviour but also in the way shops, restaurants and other businesses package and sell everyday goods.
        “As a longtime resident of Islamabad, I’m tired of seeing plastic bags littering our beautiful parks and streets. Switching to reusable bags would make such a difference in keeping our city clean and green for everyone,” said Naseem, a housewife in Sector G-7.
         For retailers, however, the transition can be more complicated.
          “As a shopkeeper in Islamabad, I’ve noticed most customers still prefer plastic bags because the reusable ones cost more and some people forget to bring them. The Plastic-Free Islamabad campaign is a good idea, but it will only work if alternative bags are made cheaper and easily available for small shops like mine,” said Raheem, a local vendor at Aabpara Market in G-6.
              The issue is equally relevant to younger residents, who authorities hope will adopt environmentally responsible habits as part of their daily routines.
         “As a student in Islamabad, I’ve started carrying a reusable bag everywhere so I don’t have to take plastic ones from shops. If more of us do the same, our parks, campuses and streets will stay much cleaner,” said Sawaira, a BS Media Studies student at NUML University.
         Food businesses face another set of challenges, particularly because takeaway packaging has to meet requirements related to hygiene, convenience and customer expectations.
           “Running a small restaurant in Islamabad, I’ve tried switching to paper and biodegradable packaging, but the higher cost is tough when customers still expect cheap takeaway. Practical alternatives only work if suppliers make them affordable and people are willing to pay a little extra for a cleaner city,” said Asif, a restaurant owner in F-10.
         The renewed campaign is not being launched in a regulatory vacuum.
         The Pakistan Environmental Protection Agency (Pak-EPA) said the Single-Use Plastics (Prohibition) Regulations, 2023, already prohibit the manufacture, import, sale, distribution, storage and use of polythene bags and other banned single-use plastics across the Islamabad Capital Territory.
         A Pak-EPA spokesperson said the agency’s enforcement would continue through regular market inspections, confiscation of banned materials, sealing of non-compliant outlets and legal action against violators.
        According to the spokesperson, penalties range from Rs5,000 for individuals to Rs10,000–50,000 for shopkeepers, while manufacturers and wholesalers can face penalties of up to Rs500,000.
         The agency said limited exemptions were available for authorised industrial packing, municipal waste, hospital waste and hazardous waste, subject to prior approval from Pak-EPA.
        “Our enforcement priority is clear and ongoing: regular market inspections, confiscation of banned materials, sealing of non-compliant outlets and legal action against violators,” the spokesperson said.
          The agency also urged businesses to shift towards affordable reusable and biodegradable alternatives and called on citizens to carry their own bags and cooperate with enforcement efforts.
           The campaign’s effectiveness, however, is likely to depend on how easily consumers and businesses can make the transition. While awareness about the environmental impact of plastic is increasing, convenience and cost continue to influence the choices of both consumers and businesses.
             For a household, carrying a reusable bag may be a relatively simple change. For a small retailer, replacing thousands of plastic bags can add to operating costs. Restaurants face similar concerns when replacing plastic containers and other disposable packaging with more expensive alternatives.
              For many small businesses, the availability of affordable alternatives could therefore determine whether the campaign succeeds in the long term.
          If reusable and biodegradable products remain significantly more expensive, shopkeepers and restaurant owners may find it difficult to make the switch without passing the additional cost on to customers.
          Consumers, meanwhile, may also need to change established habits. Many shoppers accept plastic bags automatically when making purchases, particularly for small or unexpected purchases.
         Carrying reusable bags regularly could reduce demand for single-use alternatives and make environmentally responsible choices part of everyday life.
           The authorities have said the campaign is intended not only to discourage single-use plastic but also to create greater awareness about its environmental impact and encourage responsible waste disposal.
          CDA Chairman and Chief Commissioner Islamabad Sohail Ashraf has described making Islamabad plastic-free as a shared responsibility rather than merely an enforcement exercise, stressing the need for cooperation among residents, traders, businesses, educational institutions and government agencies.
           The administration is also seeking to link the campaign with broader cleanliness and waste-management objectives. Officials say reducing plastic waste can help keep roads, markets, parks and public spaces cleaner and reduce the amount of plastic entering drainage systems.
              Plastic waste can be particularly visible in Islamabad’s green spaces, where bags and disposable packaging can accumulate around roadside areas, parks and markets. During rainfall, improperly discarded plastic can also enter drains and contribute to blockages, adding another challenge for the city’s waste-management system.
               For Islamabad, a city whose identity is closely associated with its green spaces, the issue is increasingly visible in everyday life from plastic bags caught in roadside vegetation to disposable packaging accumulating around markets and public areas.
         The challenge now is to turn the campaign from an enforcement exercise into a sustained change in consumption habits. Regular inspections and penalties may discourage businesses from using banned materials, but lasting results will require consumers to change their behaviour as well.
            That could mean a resident remembering to carry a reusable bag, a student refusing unnecessary packaging, a shopkeeper finding an affordable alternative or a restaurant absorbing or sharing the additional cost of environmentally friendly packaging.
             Schools, universities and other educational institutions could also play an important role by encouraging students to avoid unnecessary plastic and promoting reusable products. Similarly, businesses could help by making alternative packaging more visible and accessible to customers.
                Ultimately, the success of the “Plastic-Free Islamabad” campaign may depend on whether these small individual choices become routine and whether affordable alternatives are available to make those choices practical for both consumers and businesses.
            The fight against plastic will not end with inspections or fines. It will be won through everyday choices. If residents, businesses and authorities act together, Islamabad can protect its green identity and build a cleaner future for generations to come.

title: South Punjab’s cities cry out for much-needed pedestrian pathways
text:
A lack of proper pedestrian pathways in cities across South Punjab is turning walking into a daily struggle for residents, pushing many to rely on motorcycles even for short, everyday journeys.
South Punjab’s cities cry out for much-needed pedestrian pathways
Muhammad Atif Ismail
MULTAN, October 4 (APP) :A lack of proper pedestrian pathways in cities across South Punjab is turning walking into a daily struggle for residents, pushing many to rely on motorcycles even for short, everyday journeys.
       From visiting a nearby shop to buying vegetables or travelling to work, people often struggle to walk safely along busy roads where footpaths are missing, poorly maintained or buried under encroachments, leaving pedestrians exposed to traffic and making even the shortest journey a difficult and risky experience.
        As a result, walking is gradually losing its place in daily urban life, while motorcycles have become a common choice for even the shortest trips.
          Across Urban South Punjab, only some roads have designated footpaths and even these do not always provide a continuous and accessible route. In many places, pedestrians encounter broken surfaces, parked motorcycles, shop displays and other obstructions that leave little room to walk.
         On roads without footpaths, they are often forced to share space with moving traffic, making routine journeys uncomfortable and potentially dangerous.
         For many residents, walking has consequently become an activity reserved mainly for parks rather than a practical way to reach nearby destinations.
           People can be seen exercising in parks during the morning and evening, but considerably fewer appear to choose walking for ordinary tasks such as visiting a market, going to a shop or travelling to a nearby workplace.
          Muhammad Rashid Qureshi, a resident of Pul Bararan (Multan), says he usually walks in a park but uses his motorcycle even when going out to buy vegetables.
         “Many roads do not have footpaths. Even where they exist, they are often not properly maintained. In several places, encroachments leave almost no space for pedestrians,” he says.
         He adds that walking along busy roads makes him feel uneasy because he remains concerned about the possibility of an accident involving passing traffic.
      His experience highlights a practical problem faced by many urban residents: walking may be a convenient option in terms of distance, but the absence of safe pedestrian routes can make it an unattractive choice.
        Muhammad Amjad, another citizen from Nawabpur road, points to Bosan Road, one of the city’s major thoroughfares, where footpaths are present along some stretches but missing from others.
          Despite the road’s considerable width, he says, the lack of continuous pedestrian pathways makes walking difficult. He also believes that the growing number of motorcycles has contributed to a change in people’s daily habits.
          Amjad describes this change as a cultural shift, arguing that people increasingly prefer motorcycles even for short journeys. However, he stresses that walking remains important for personal health and that residents need suitable infrastructure if they are to make it part of their everyday routines.
            His observations raise an important question: can people be encouraged to walk when the streets around them offer little safe space to do so?
           The issue goes beyond individual preferences. A road designed primarily to accommodate moving and parked vehicles serve motorists while creating difficulties for people travelling on foot.
            The availability of a footpath on one section of a road is not enough if it ends abruptly, is blocked by encroachments or fails to connect pedestrians safely to shops, markets, public transport stops and other
destinations.
            For older people, children, persons with disabilities and those accompanying young children, these gaps can make walking particularly challenging. Broken surfaces, missing ramps, unsafe crossings and poor street lighting can further limit access to public spaces.
        The shortage of pedestrian pathways also has implications for public health. Walking to nearby destinations provides an opportunity to incorporate physical activity into daily life without setting aside a separate time for exercise. When people depend on motorcycles for almost every journey, some of these opportunities may be lost.
           This is particularly relevant for people living with diabetes and other conditions for which regular physical activity can form part of a healthy lifestyle. Parks remain valuable places for exercise, but safe footpaths can help people remain active during ordinary daily routines as well.
            The environmental impact is another consideration, said Muhammad Adnan Jandran, an environmentalist. Motorcycles and other vehicles contribute to fuel consumption, traffic emissions and noise. Although road transport is only one part of the wider urban pollution problem, making short journeys on foot a realistic option could help reduce some unnecessary motorized trips, he suggested.
              Adnan, however, expecting residents to change their habits without improving street conditions would overlook a central part of the problem. Public awareness about walking and healthy lifestyles can have limited effect when people cannot reach their destinations safely on foot.
            Multan Development Authority (MDA) says it conducts regular operations against encroachments and has a dedicated wing working to address the issue.
         Such action can help restore public space, but maintaining pedestrian access also requires regular monitoring, repairs and measures to prevent cleared footpaths from being occupied again.
        The responsibilities of urban development authorities, municipal bodies and other relevant departments need to be clearly coordinated. New road projects should provide appropriate pedestrian facilities, while existing roads require assessments to identify missing pathways, dangerous crossings and sections obstructed by encroachments.
         Footpaths also need to be designed for practical use. Continuous, level and accessible pathways, supported by safe crossings and suitable street lighting, can make walking easier for a wider range of residents. Where space is limited, authorities need to plan how roads can safely accommodate pedestrians alongside other users.
          Similarly, shopkeepers, vendors and vehicle owners also have a role in keeping pedestrian routes clear. At the same time, authorities need consistent enforcement and practical arrangements for parking and commercial activity so that public pathways remain available for their intended purpose.
       Better pedestrian infrastructure can also support public transport. People travelling by bus or other shared services often need to walk to and from their stops. If these routes are blocked or unsafe, using public transport becomes less convenient, even when the service itself is available.
      For South Punjab’s cities including Vehari, Khanewal, Loudhran, Muzaffargarh, Layyah and others, the challenge is therefore not simply to build more roads or accommodate more vehicles. It is also to ensure that residents can move around their neighbourhoods safely, including when they choose to walk.
        The experiences shared by Rashid Qureshi and Amjad suggest that the growing reliance on motorcycles cannot be understood solely as a matter of personal preference. The condition and availability of pedestrian pathways also influence the choices people make every day.
          For South Punjab’s urban centers, restoring space for pedestrians is not merely a matter of road design. It is an opportunity to make everyday journeys safer, support healthier lifestyles and create streets that serve people on foot as well as those travelling on two wheels.

title: Maldives President Mohamed Muizzu arrive in Pakistan on state visit
text:
Published October 20, 2026
ISLAMABAD: Maldives President Dr Mohamed Muizzu arrived in Pakistan on Tuesday for a three-day state visit at the invitation of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
Dr Muizzu was accompanied by First Lady Madam Sajidha Mohamed and a high-level delegation comprising cabinet ministers and senior officials.
Upon arrival at Islamabad International Airport, the Maldives president and the first lady were accorded a 21-gun salute.
According to a statement issued by the Prime Minister's Office, Dr Muizzu will be accorded an official welcome tomorrow at the Prime Minister’s House.
The visiting dignitary is on a state visit to Pakistan from October 20 to 22.
During the visit, President Muizzu will meet his Pakistani counterpart Asif Ali Zardari, who will also host a State Banquet in his honour. He will also hold restricted and delegation-level talks with PM Shehbaz.
A Foreign Office spokesperson had earlier said that the two leaders would review the entire spectrum of bilateral relations and explore avenues to further strengthen cooperation in trade, investment, health, education, tourism, agriculture, defence, maritime security, climate change and people-to-people exchanges.
They will also exchange views on regional and international developments of mutual interest.
“The visit will also feature a Pakistan–Maldives Business Forum, aimed at promoting greater interaction between the business communities of the two countries and exploring new opportunities for trade and investment. A number of agreements and Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs) covering diverse areas of bilateral cooperation are expected to be signed during the visit,” read the statement.
The state visit, the first by a President of Maldives to Pakistan in eleven years, assumes special significance as the two countries commemorate the 60th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations in 1966.
Pakistan and Maldives enjoyed warm and fraternal relations rooted in shared faith, mutual respect, longstanding goodwill and close cooperation at regional and international forums.
The spokesperson had said that the visit reflects the shared commitment of both countries to further strengthen their bilateral partnership and open new avenues of mutually beneficial cooperation.

title: Mir Raza murder case shows 'epic failure' in police investigation: judicial commission
text:
Published October 20, 2026
KARACHI: A judicial commission investigating the death of Mir Raza Ali has described the police investigation as an “epic failure”, finding serious lapses ranging from negligence and poor supervision to a failure to preserve evidence and pursue the case professionally.
The single-member commission, headed by Sindh High Court judge Justice Omar Sial, said police breached required procedures necessary to withstand judicial scrutiny and support a successful prosecution, according to the executive summary, submitted to Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah on October 15.
The commission was constituted by the Sindh government to examine the circumstances surrounding the death of 25-year-old Mir Raza, assess the impartiality of police and medico-legal investigations and identify any professional negligence, misconduct, manipulation of evidence or cover-up.
Mir Raza, an IBA graduate who ran a waffle-making business, left his PECHS home in the early hours of July 28. His family reported him missing the same day, while his body was recovered the following morning within the jurisdiction of Gulistan-e-Johar police station.
In its assessment of police conduct, the commission found a lack of leadership, seriousness and supervision, as well as negligence by senior officers in some instances.
“The handling of this case has been like a rudderless ship, not aware of its destination,” the report observed.
It described the investigation as ranging from “negligent to criminally negligent”, as well as inexplicable, casual and unprofessional.
Significantly, the commission said an active cover-up during the initial stages of the investigation could not be conclusively ruled out, while senior police officers had swept clear investigative lapses “under the carpet” instead of acknowledging or addressing them.
The report also accused senior officers of “tunnel vision”, saying they became so focused on a single objective that they failed to see the bigger picture.
It said police, driven by ego and a desire to avoid publicly admitting an error, doubled down on their initial suicide theory rather than investigating further.
According to the commission, dozens of authorised and unauthorised police officers became involved in collecting evidence and approaching and interrogating crucial individuals, often without documenting their actions.
The result, it said, was that no officer was willing to take responsibility for the lapses, with responsibility instead shifted to subordinates or the shortcomings denied altogether.
The commission further criticised police communication, saying neither the family nor the public was kept informed through official disclosures. Police also failed to follow its recommendation to appoint a focal person, contributing to further public speculation.
The report noted that police initially raised suicide as the cause of Mir Raza’s death, but his family questioned the conclusion after observing what they said were visible torture marks.
Following concerns raised by the police surgeon over anomalies in the first post-mortem report, the body was exhumed on August 8. The final official report later confirmed the cause of death as a perforating firearm injury from the back, ruling out suicide. Murder and destruction-of-evidence provisions were subsequently added to the FIR.
The commission said the police hypothesis had relied on unconfirmed and unsubstantiated text messages, selective video footage and the first post-mortem report, which itself had not concluded that Mir Raza died by suicide.
It said the bullet trajectory, wound characteristics, absence of blood, condition of the body, acid burns and anaesthesia detected in the blood excluded suicide.
“The police investigation failed in its most basic duty: to establish the truth,” the commission concluded, adding that the post-mortem findings left no doubt that Mir Raza was murdered.
Turning to the way forward, the commission said the case had reached a “critical juncture”, with public trust in the police severely damaged.
It found that a significant portion of physical evidence had been compromised, meaning the case could now only be resolved through a rigorous, intelligence-based investigation.
The commission recommended that police transparently acknowledge and apologise for past operational lapses and immediately initiate formal inquiries against officers responsible for them.
It also recommended accepting the family’s request for a Joint Investigation Team, describing a JIT as the “most viable path” in the extraordinary circumstances.
The proposed JIT should be headed by DIG Irfan Baloch and include senior representatives of the Inter-Services Intelligence, Intelligence Bureau, Pakistan Rangers (Sindh) and National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency to ensure an impartial and comprehensive investigation.
Separately, the commission recommended a high-level committee, preferably led by the Federal Investigation Agency, to determine whether police officials involved in the first 10 days of the probe violated Sections 201, 166(2) and 218 of the Pakistan Penal Code.
The committee should initiate criminal action, alongside disciplinary proceedings, against any officials found culpable, it recommended.
The commission stressed, however, that it did not itself possess investigative powers and therefore could not conclusively determine that an active cover-up had occurred, although it said certain “inexplicable actions” raised the possibility of one at some stage.

title: PTI rules out Achakzai's removal, says no talks on making Fazl opposition leader
text:
Published October 20, 2026
ISLAMABAD: PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan on Monday ruled out any “minus” for Mahmood Khan Achakzai, saying there had also been no discussion about replacing him with JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman as opposition leader in the National Assembly.
Speaking to Geo News at Parliament House, Gohar said PTI founder Imran Khan had complete confidence in Achakzai and that the party had no authority to decide whether to accept the opposition leader or not.
“We accept the PTI founder’s decision and will move forward accordingly,” he said.
Gohar said everyone in the party was free to express their opinion, but once the party made a decision, it was accepted by all.
He said the decision regarding the opposition leader was at Imran’s discretion, adding that the PTI founder had named Achakzai and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas as leaders and directed the party to move forward under their guidance.
“The PTI founder gave me instructions, and those are what we accept and follow,” Gohar said, adding that neither opposition leader had been disrespected.
He said everything was proceeding at the PTI founder’s discretion, adding: “If there had to be a ‘minus’, it would have happened by now.”
Gohar also maintained that Imran could not be “minus”, claiming that 90% of the nation currently stood with him.
Separately, the PTI chairman said he had spoken to National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq about production orders for 10 arrested parliamentarians.
He said lawmakers Adil Bazai and Chaudhry Imtiaz had been arrested and that the speaker had been informed about the arrests.
Gohar also confirmed that Mishal Yousafzai had been issued a show-cause notice, describing it as an internal party matter.
In a separate conversation with the media on Adiala Road in Rawalpindi, Gohar claimed that the demand for a meeting with Imran was what led to the imposition of governor’s rule.
“We oppose terrorism in all its forms,” he said, adding that PTI had joined talks with the government unconditionally.
“We went to get our prayers granted, but instead ended up having to fast,” Gohar remarked, using an Urdu proverb to describe the outcome of the talks.
He said PTI had a government in only one province and that too had been “snatched away”.
Gohar said political interests should not be protected under the guise of terrorism, adding that PTI still wanted the National Action Plan to be implemented.
“The government has done what it wanted to do. It should now reverse it,” he said.
Rejecting claims that PTI’s negotiating committee was receiving instructions from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Gohar said he was unaware of any mention of consulting Murad Saeed during the negotiations.
He reiterated that there had been no discussion about making Fazlur Rehman the opposition leader.
“Mahmood Achakzai has been given authority by the PTI founder. There can be no discussion on that,” Gohar said.
Gohar also recalled meeting Imran three times on November 25, 2024 — in the morning, afternoon and at night.
He said he spoke to former KP CM Ali Amin Gandapur over the phone during one of the meetings, during which Gandapur asked Imran to record a video statement.
According to Gohar, he later received a call from Adiala asking him to return because Imran wanted to record the video. He said he reached Adiala at midnight.
Gohar said Imran wanted to offer condolences over the martyrdom of Rangers personnel in the video and had not refused to record the statement.
However, according to Gohar, Imran wanted the recording to be made on Gohar’s mobile phone to prevent any tampering. Gohar said his phone was with jail authorities, while the device available to record the statement belonged to them.
He added that Imran asked Gandapur to remain where he was and told Gohar to return the following day to record the video.
Gohar also claimed that a statement attributed to now-dysfunctional KP CM Sohail Afridi regarding Pakistan’s flag had been generated using artificial intelligence.

title: DPM Dar stresses Afghanistan's stability for regional peace at SCO moot
text:
Published October 20, 2026
ISLAMABAD: Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Tuesday stressed that stability in Afghanistan is imperative for safeguarding peace and stability in the region.
Addressing the narrow-format session of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Council of Heads of Government meeting in Dushanbe, Tajikistan, the DPM said that Pakistan continues to be desirous of a peaceful, stable, regionally integrated and prosperous Afghanistan, which is at peace with itself and its neighbours.
“We have made sincere efforts to support Afghanistan's development and the well-being of its people,” the top diplomat said, adding that Islamabad has only one expectation from the Afghan Taliban regime, in return, that Afghan territory should not be used for terrorism against Pakistan or the rest of the world.
“Sustainable economic development cannot be guaranteed without durable peace and security in the region,” he added.
The DPM said that Pakistan remains committed to a peaceful and stable neighbourhood as an essential foundation for regional development and prosperity.
Since the Afghan Taliban returned to power in 2021, Pakistan has witnessed a sharp rise in cross-border terrorist incidents, particularly in KP and Balochistan.
Pakistan recorded its highest monthly number of terrorist attacks in 12 years during September 2026. Islamabad has repeatedly urged Kabul to prevent its territory from being used by militant organisations to carry out attacks inside Pakistan.
Pakistan maintains that the Afghan Taliban regime has failed to take effective action against groups responsible for attacks on Pakistani security forces and civilians.
Addressing the moot, the DPM said: “For our region to achieve seamless economic integration, targeted investments in core sectors, most notably in energy and transport, are vital.
He said that Pakistan strongly advocates for expanding investments into high-potential industries, including agriculture, mining and minerals, and information technology, to build a resilient and interconnected economic future for all our nations.
The deputy prime minister said that the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) offers every SCO partner a compelling opportunity to participate in and accelerate our shared journey toward comprehensive economic integration.
Pakistan also believes that Artificial Intelligence, digital transformation, innovation, energy cooperation and international information security should become important pillars of future cooperation within the SCO, he added.
With these priorities in mind, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif unveiled Pakistan's vision for its SCO Chairmanship under the theme "Turning Vision into Action: Connectivity, Innovation and Shared Prosperity", Dar said.
The DPM said: “We reiterate the need to accelerate efforts to promote the use of national currencies for mutual settlement and establishing the SCO Development Bank, SCO Development Fund and an Investment Fund. Such tools and measures will advance development initiatives and help the SCO region to offset international financial shocks.

title: Sindh raises age limit for CCE exams to 33 years
text:
Published October 20, 2026
KARACHI: The Sindh cabinet has approved an increase in the upper age limit for the Combined Competitive Examination (CCE) from 30 to 33 years, while also increasing the number of attempts allowed for the examination from three to five.
