title: Idlib pomegranate farmers seek new markets to sell surplus harvest
text:
Idlib pomegranate farmers seek new markets to sell surplus harvest
- By Web Desk -
- Oct 19, 2026
IDLIB: Syrian pomegranate farmers in the town of Darkush, in northwestern Idlib province near the Turkish border, are struggling to bring an expected strong harvest to market amid rising production and transportation costs, low prices and limited export opportunities.
According to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA), the challenges are squeezing farmers’ incomes despite expectations of a good harvest this season.
Pomegranate cultivation is a key source of livelihood for farmers in Darkush, which lies in a valley in the Orontes River basin, at the foothills of the Syrian Coastal Mountain Range.
Farmers are calling for affordable agricultural supplies, cold storage facilities and access to new markets to help them sell their produce and improve their earnings.
Pomegranate orchards cover more than 250 hectares in Darkush, according to the local Agricultural Extension Division. The harvest of early varieties began in the second half of September, with production expected to be good this season.
Mohammad Dada, an agricultural supervisor at the Darkush Agricultural Extension Division, said field visits were being conducted to advise farmers on harvesting, packaging and controlling pests, including aphids and fungal diseases.
More than 70 per cent of farmers in the area depend on pomegranate cultivation, Dada said. However, current selling prices are insufficient to cover rising costs of pesticides, labour, packaging and transportation.
Producing one kilogramme of pomegranates costs around 50 Syrian pounds, equivalent to $0.41, he said, calling for subsidised fertilisers and pesticides to ease the financial burden on farmers.
Farmer Mohammad Sharif said pomegranate cultivation was deeply rooted in Darkush’s heritage. Some varieties are used to produce pomegranate molasses and juice, enabling producers to diversify their products and make better use of the harvest.
Farmer Nima Adeeb Nima said five main pomegranate varieties were grown in Darkush: Nab Al-Jamal, Asfouri, Al-Helu, Al-Laban and French. Early varieties are harvested from mid-September to early October.
However, limited export opportunities and restricted access to foreign markets have hurt sales, while domestic markets are unable to absorb the entire harvest, he said.
Read More: PM Shehbaz meets Syrian president, offers support for economic recovery
Trader Samer Bakro said transportation costs, particularly fuel prices, had made it more expensive to ship pomegranates to Damascus and other provinces.
Renting a vehicle costs around $130, he said, adding that more export channels were needed to sell surplus produce, which also faces limited storage options.
Expanding export opportunities and improving storage facilities could help farmers and traders reduce losses, reach new markets and secure better returns from the harvest.

title: Oil slips from 5-month high as Trump's Russia sanctions waiver may bring more supplies
text:
Oil slips from 5-month high as Trump's Russia sanctions waiver may bring more supplies
- By Reuters -
- Oct 19, 2026
SINGAPORE: Oil prices slipped from a five-month high on Monday as investors took profits after US President Donald Trump waived sanctions and tariffs on Russia that may lead to more Russian fuel exports.
Brent crude futures fell $2.29, or 2.08%, to $107.57 a barrel by 0619 GMT after settling at its highest since May 19 on Friday.
US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $99.46 a barrel, down $1.95, or 1.92%, after closing at its highest since September 17 on Friday.
Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving key sanctions and tariffs under the law known as the Graham Act, which he signed last month at the urging of lawmakers who wanted to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
However, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the president will use up to 60 days to assess the impact of the sanctions and tariffs on the global economy.
“Trump’s move looks like another desperate attempt to keep oil prices in check ahead of the US midterm elections,” said Priyanka Sachdeva, head of market insight at Phillip Nova, adding that it does little to address the physical supply disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, where oil tanker attacks continue.
KCM Trade chief analyst Tim Waterer said while the US waiver on Russian sanctions could lead to higher Russian fuel exports, the mixed messaging has created uncertainty.
“Until the details and duration are clearer, the market is unlikely to fully price in a sustained increase in supply,” he added.
The waiver comes after Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to export diesel to the United States and other countries — starting at about 2.3 million barrels this month before rising to about 7.6 million barrels monthly. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said these US actions will hurt Ukraine.
MIDDLE EAST CRUDE EXPORTS FALL SHARPLY
Brent crude oil briefly touched $110 a barrel on Friday for the first time since May as tensions and security threats in the Middle East raised concerns over the safety of shipping and tighter global energy supplies.
Intensified attacks on commercial vessels cut Gulf crude flows sharply to about 8.5 million barrels per day on a seven-day average last week from more than 20 million bpd the week before, analytics firm Kpler said in a note on Friday. At least 10 confirmed incidents involving commercial vessels were reported last week, it added.
Potentially raising the stakes in the Middle East war, Egypt said it is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security and stability against Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis.
DBS expects oil prices to remain rangebound in the $100 to $110 a barrel range going into the US midterms as Iran and its proxies would ensure oil prices and domestic fuel prices remain the key irritant for US voters.
“The US president is trying various moves to suppress prices ahead of the midterms without any direct concession to Iran,” its head of energy research Suvro Sarkar said.
“However, all the levers he has pulled – including waivers on Russia sanctions – are short-term fixes and will have barely any structural impact on the supply situation.”

title: Macron calls for order after ‘unbridled violence’ across France
text:
Macron calls for order after ‘unbridled violence’ across France
- By Web Desk -
- Oct 19, 2026
PARIS: French President Emmanuel Macron has criticized “unbridled violence” after one of the most violent days of unrest in years left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,400 people arrested in cities across the country.
“Watching these images, we have all asked ourselves how could French people do this to France?” he said in a televised address to the nation from the Élysée Palace.
Macron called for “calm and order” and said “nothing justifies” violence and that local state officials would be able to ban certain street gatherings if they deemed it necessary.
He said a distinction must be drawn between what he called genuine, peaceful demonstrators making demands over the cost of living and the education system, and others who “destroy, ransack and loot”.
He criticized what he called “fractious groups from the ultra-left, joined by numerous delinquents”.
Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for largely peaceful protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Police have arrested about 2,400 people, according to France’s interior ministry.
Politicians on the left and right called for the resignation of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez after the government appeared to have been caught by surprise by the scale of violence on Saturday as state buildings were stormed and torched, bus stops smashed, roads barricaded and shops broken into and destroyed.
Crowds clashed with police at Place de la République in central Paris on Sunday afternoon as violence flared for a second day. Electric bikes were piled in some streets and set alight.
Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings.
Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people in Paris, according to the AFP news agency, and bottles and rocks were again hurled at police.
Sunday saw cities across the country confront the impact of what developed into one of the worst bouts of disorder in modern French history.
In Limoges, the ornate 19th-century city hall was gutted by a fire started by rioters on Saturday, its clock tower and roof collapsing and the flames took hold.
Shopkeepers were seen early on Sunday morning picking up large shards of glass in Paris as rubbish trucks cleared up debris on some of the larger streets.
Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas.
Macron said local prefects and mayors would draft measures to protect shops and civic buildings.
The president also said there would be “full transparency” over the police response to the demonstrations.
Tear gas and water cannons were turned on crowds over the weekend and riot police were seen hitting people with batons in several places.
France’s interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously.
Student protests which began last month escalated significantly on Saturday after they were joined by trade union members and other anti-government groups.
The response from political figures has pointed to France’s deep political divisions as the country prepares for an election in April which could see the hard-right pitted against the hard-left.
France’s Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that while demonstrating was a fundamental right, there were “outrages” committed by “several thousand far-left individuals” who were determined to target public buildings and confront the police.
Later, they were joined by “delinquents who looted and ransacked numerous businesses in several cities in France”, he said.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the hard-left La France Insoumise party, heavily criticised Nuñez and police chiefs on social media.
He said they had “shown complete incompetence” with their handling of the demonstrations and called them “specialists in organised chaos”.
Meanwhile, the leader of the hard-right National Rally party, Marine Le Pen, condemned the “exploitation” of anger “by political forces that encourage violence”.

title: Saudi Arabia introduces live crowd updates to help Umrah pilgrims avoid congestion at Two Holy mosques
text:
Saudi Arabia introduces live crowd updates to help Umrah pilgrims avoid congestion at Two Holy mosques
DUBAI: Saudi Arabia has introduced digital services that allow Umrah pilgrims to monitor crowd levels in real time at the Grand Mosque in Mecca and the Prophet’s Mosque in Medina, helping them choose less congested times to perform their rituals.
The services provide live displays, instant updates and crowd indicators for the Tawaf area around the Holy Kaaba and the Sa’i walkway between Safa and Marwa, enabling pilgrims to assess congestion before heading to the mosque.
An interactive map covering the Grand Mosque in Mecca and the Prophet’s Mosque in Medina also allows worshippers and visitors to explore landmarks, locate facilities and identify suitable routes, making navigation easier and improving their overall experience.
The digital platform features approximately 950 points of interest and landmarks, including the Holy Kaaba, Maqam Ibrahim, Safa and Marwa at the Grand Mosque.
At the Prophet’s Mosque, the map highlights prominent sites such as Al Rawdah Al Sharifah, the Prophet’s Chamber, prayer niches and the Prophet’s pulpit.
The platform offers more than 100,000 possible routes across over 17 categories, helping users locate facilities and services according to their needs.
It also provides more than 650 QR codes, allowing visitors to quickly access information about landmarks, facilities and available services.
The interactive map is integrated with more than six on-site digital display screens, enabling visitors to view locations and routes directly while at the mosques.
The system also caters to people with disabilities by identifying accessible landmarks and suitable routes, alongside tools designed to support inclusive access.
The initiative forms part of efforts to enhance the experience of pilgrims and worshippers through digital technology, improve crowd management and facilitate movement within Islam’s two holiest mosques.

title: More than 23,000 votes cast in Edmonton Khalistan referendum
text:
More than 23,000 votes cast in Edmonton Khalistan referendum
- By Jahanzaib Ali -
- Oct 19, 2026
EDMONTON, Alberta: More than 23,000 votes were cast Sunday in a Khalistan referendum in Edmonton, according to organizers, who extended voting hours to accommodate people waiting in long lines.
Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, general counsel of Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), announced a strategy he described as fifth-generation warfare aimed at removing Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government from power.
He also said the organization would launch a campaign on Nov. 1 to register 2 million voters for the Khalistan referendum.
The Punjab Referendum Commission (PRC), which oversaw the voting process, extended polling hours beyond the scheduled closing time to allow people still in line to cast their ballots.
Addressing a large gathering at the event, Pannun outlined a three-pronged strategy to advance the movement for an independent Sikh homeland in Punjab.
It includes mobilizing voters through referendums worldwide, supporting political and youth movements opposing Modi’s government within India, and increasing international economic pressure on the country.
SFJ announces voter registration campaign
Pannun said the voter registration drive would begin Nov. 1, a date SFJ commemorates as a day of remembrance for the 1984 anti-Sikh violence.
He said the campaign would run alongside the electoral process for Punjab’s state assembly.
Read More: UN experts urge Canada to protect threatened Sikh activist
Describing the political component of the strategy, Pannun said SFJ was providing financial assistance and support to CJP and youth movements seeking to challenge Modi’s government.
He presented the effort as part of a broader campaign to advance the cause of Punjab’s independence.
Pannun also urged foreign investors to withdraw investments from Indian markets, describing the move as a way to increase economic pressure on the Modi government.
He argued that removing Modi’s government from power would represent a step toward Punjab’s independence.
Pannun accuses Modi government over Sikh leader’s killing
Pannun referred to the killing of Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Canada and accused the Modi government of using force to obstruct the Khalistan referendum movement.
He called for accountability for Modi, Indian Home Minister Amit Shah, External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, national security adviser Ajit Doval and Samant Goel.
Modi visits to Canada, U.S.
Commenting on possible visits by Modi to Canada and the United States in December, Pannun said the Indian prime minister would face opposition from the Khalistan movement in both countries.
The visits were described as possible, rather than confirmed, in the remarks provided by the organizers.
Proposed Sikh homeland security force
Pannun renewed his appeal for Sikh youth around the world to obtain firearms training within the law and join a proposed Sikh Homeland Security (SHS) defensive force.
He said the proposed force would focus on the lawful protection of the Sikh community and defensive preparedness.
Concluding his remarks, Pannun said Modi’s political career began in Punjab and that his political defeat would also come there.

title: Last time you wanted to finish the job': Iranian foreign minister challenges Donald Trump
text:
Last time you wanted to finish the job': Iranian foreign minister challenges Donald Trump
- By Web Desk -
- Oct 19, 2026
TEHRAN: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has hit back at US President Donald Trump’s threat to “finish the job” against Tehran, warning Washington against military confrontation while accusing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of pushing the United States into a war for his own political survival.
“Last time you wanted to ‘finish the job’, Iran emerged even stronger. Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful, we have unfinished jobs too,” Araghchi posted on X.
The Iranian foreign minister further claimed that Netanyahu was attempting to drag Washington into another conflict to avoid facing legal consequences in Israel, warning of serious repercussions. “Netanyahu is driving America into another war to stay out of jail, whatever the consequences for Israel — let alone POTUS,” Araghchi wrote.
The war of words follows Trump’s robust endorsement of Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s October 27 parliamentary election via Truth Social. Praising Netanyahu as a “Great Warrior Prime Minister” and a vital partner for peace, Trump warned that the US could take matters into its own hands if Israeli voters chose a different leader. Claiming that Iran has been systematically weakened, Trump warned that Washington would soon “finish the job” unless Tehran changed course.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran, with its 51 year old chant, “Death to Israel, Death to America! We will destroy the Little Satan and the Big Satan.” What Country can survive when things such as this are allowed to be said, because eventually, they always end up being true? It would have been only a question of time until Iran would have put that ominous phrase into effect, but they have been systematically destroyed, both Militarily and Financially, and unless they change their ways, rapidly, we will soon finish the job…” Trump wrote.

title: Macron notes 'failures' after France unrest
text:
Macron notes 'failures' after France unrest
- By AFP -
- Oct 19, 2026
PARIS: President Emmanuel Macron, under pressure after violent protests in France, acknowledged on Monday “failures in anticipation and intelligence”, but refused the resignation of his interior minister, the presidential palace said.
Some opposition politicians had called for the sacking of Nunez after demonstrations over the cost of living descended into some of the worst urban violence in France in years.
Nearly 2,400 people were arrested on Saturday, with almost 1,000 police and gendarmes injured, according to the interior ministry, as clashes between police and protesters, mass looting and fires erupted nationwide.
“The interior minister submitted his resignation to the president on Sunday,” the Elysee palace said in a statement.
“Given the necessity for continued leadership of law enforcement at this time, the president refused.”
Macron had asked Nunez to “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over the failures in planning and intelligence that led to the violence”, the statement said.
The president had also instructed him to “put in place new operational methods for security forces” to handle the crisis.

title: Texas Democrats eye breakthrough as Republicans face voter anger
text:
Texas Democrats eye breakthrough as Republicans face voter anger
- By AFP -
- Oct 19, 2026
SAN ANTONIO, United States: After more than three decades of Republican dominance, Democrats in Texas see a rare chance to break through in November’s midterm elections, as voter anger over immigration raids and the cost-of-living tests US President Donald Trump’s support.
No Democrat has won statewide office in the conservative southern state since 1994, and Trump carried Texas by nearly 14 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election.
But with a US Senate seat and the governorship at stake on November 3, recent polls suggest Republicans face an unusually competitive challenge.
At the forefront is James Talarico, a 37-year-old former teacher and state lawmaker whose blend of Christian faith, economic populism and appeals for political unity has helped make the Senate race one of the country’s most closely watched.
A University of Texas poll released this week put Talarico ahead of Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general and a staunch Trump ally, by 50 percent to 47 percent — a lead within the survey’s margin of error.
A separate UMass Lowell poll found the two candidates tied.
A Presbyterian seminarian, Talarico has sought to attract independents and Republicans disillusioned with Trump, arguing that Texans have more in common than the country’s increasingly bitter political divisions suggest.
“I’ll always put Texas before any political party,” he has said.
Trump, however, has campaigned aggressively for Paxton, warning at a recent rally in San Antonio that losing the seat could jeopardize the Republicans’ narrow Senate majority.
“It’s a killer in Congress because we have a very close majority. We can’t let that happen,” Trump said, mocking Talarico with the nickname “Talafreako” and accusing Democrats of wanting to reopen the country’s borders.
Paxton’s baggage
Trump backed Paxton over incumbent Senator John Cornyn in a bitter Republican primary battle, despite warnings that the attorney general’s history of controversy could imperil the party’s hold on the seat.
Paxton was impeached by the Republican-controlled Texas House in 2023 over allegations of corruption and abuse of power, although the state Senate subsequently acquitted him.
In an extraordinary twist, Dan Cogdell, one of the lawyers who defended Paxton during the proceedings, has since endorsed Talarico.
More recently, The Wall Street Journal reported that Paxton spent New Year’s Eve in Dubai with two American businessmen indicted over alleged healthcare fraud. Both have pleaded not guilty.
Yet Paxton retains support among Trump-aligned conservatives, including some who acknowledge misgivings about their candidate.
Cracks in Trump’s coalition
Beyond Paxton’s personal controversies, Democrats are looking to exploit growing discontent over immigration enforcement and the economy.
Trump’s commanding victory in Texas in 2024 owed partly to substantial gains among Latino voters, particularly along the state’s southern border with Mexico.
But some of those voters are now reconsidering their support.
Cattle industry groups in Texas, Kansas and Oklahoma have also warned that immigration raids are disrupting agricultural businesses, deterring legally employed workers and threatening to drive up beef prices.
A May survey by the Latino civil rights group UnidosUS found that one in five Texas Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 would not do so again if given another chance.
The broader discontent has also given Democrats hope in the race for governor, where three-term Republican incumbent Greg Abbott faces an unexpectedly close contest against state lawmaker Gina Hinojosa.
Hinojosa has focused her campaign on the cost of living, seeking to appeal to voters beyond the traditional Democratic base.
For Melendez, disillusionment with Trump has become reason enough to switch sides.
“I didn’t vote for Trump because I liked him,” he told AFP. “I voted for Trump to punish Biden. And I’m going to vote for the Democrat for the same reason: to punish Trump.”

title: Information ministry rejects reports of army officer’s death during Pakistan–Sri Lanka match
text:
Information ministry rejects reports of army officer’s death during Pakistan–Sri Lanka match
- By Laiq Ur Rehman -
- Oct 19, 2026
ISLAMABAD: The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting’s Fact Check account on Monday rejected reports claiming that a Pakistan Army officer died during the Pakistan–Sri Lanka cricket match at Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium, clarifying that the deceased was an employee of the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB).
A social media post had claimed that a Pakistan Army personnel died of a heart attack during the ongoing Pakistan–Sri Lanka match at the stadium.
The post stated that, according to rescue sources, 50-year-old Muhammad Farooq, son of Muhammad Azam, suddenly lost consciousness during the match and was shifted to a hospital, where he later died.
However, the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting refuted the claim in a statement shared on X, saying the deceased was a PCB employee and was not present at the stadium during the match. It added that he had no involvement in the event.
According to the ministry, the individual suffered an electric shock, following which his family contacted Rescue 1122 and he was shifted to a local hospital.
Ton-up Agha helps Pakistan down Sri Lanka in tri-series opener
The ministry said hospital records identified the cause of death as electrocution, adding that further inquiry would proceed in accordance with the prescribed procedure.
“Linking this medical emergency to the cricket match is misleading,” the statement said, clarifying that the individual’s employment with the PCB did not establish any connection between the incident and the ongoing match.
The ministry urged the public to verify information before sharing claims on social media. It also shared a report from New Town Police Station regarding the incident on social media.

Claim: An officer of the Pakistan Army passed away due to a heart attack during the ongoing Pakistan–Sri Lanka cricket match at Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium.
Fact
▪️The individual is a Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) employee. He was not present at the stadium during the match and had no involvement in the event. He suffered electric shock following which his family contacted Rescue 1122 and he was shifted to local hospital.
▪️Cause of death as per hospital record has been identified as “electrocution”. Further inquiry will proceed as per procedure.

title: NCCIA issues stern warning against fake social media profiles of women
text:
NCCIA issues stern warning against fake social media profiles of women
- By Hamid Ur Rehman -
- Oct 19, 2026
ISLAMABAD: The National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) on Monday issued a stern warning against creating fake social media profiles of women, leaking their personal data and images, and blackmailing them online.
In a statement shared on social media, the NCCIA said that blackmailing women and leaking anyone’s personal data were cybercrimes punishable under the law.
“Blackmailing women, leaking private pictures or creating fake profiles are crimes,” the agency said, urging citizens to speak out against such illegal activities and submit complaints to the NCCIA along with relevant evidence.
The agency urged citizens not to remain silent and to expose those involved in online harassment.

title: Pakistan Army Major Wajahat Waheed martyred in Pasni: ISPR
text:
Pakistan Army Major Wajahat Waheed martyred in Pasni IED blast: ISPR
- By Laiq Ur Rehman -
- Oct 19, 2026
RAWALPINDI: Pakistan Army Major Wajahat Waheed was martyred in an improvised explosive device (IED) blast during security operations in Balochistan, while four terrorists were killed in a separate operation, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said on Monday.
According to the ISPR, intelligence agencies reported the presence of multiple hideouts of Indian-sponsored Fitna Al Hindustan in the areas of Shadi Kaur in Pasni tehsil, Gwadar district, and Jattakabad in Kalat district, posing a threat to the local population.
To safeguard the local populace and clear the area of terrorists, security forces are conducting operations in these areas, the military’s media wing said.
In the first incident, security forces conducted an intelligence-based operation in Jattakabad, Kalat district, on October 18, 2026. During the operation, troops engaged the terrorists’ hideout and killed four terrorists following an intense exchange of fire. A large cache of arms and ammunition was also recovered, the ISPR said.
In a separate incident, security forces conducted a series of clearance operations in Shadi Kaur, Pasni tehsil, Gwadar district. During one of the operations, the lead force component, headed by Major Wajahat Waheed, 34, a resident of Lahore, was targeted in an IED blast.
Major Wajahat Waheed made the ultimate sacrifice in the line of duty and embraced shahadat.
The ISPR said sanitisation operations would continue to eliminate any remaining terrorists in the area.
Read More: Eight terrorists killed in security forces’ IBOs in Balochistan: ISPR
It added that the counterterrorism campaign under the vision of Azm-e-Istehkam, approved by the Federal Apex Committee on the National Action Plan, would continue at full pace. Security forces and law enforcement agencies remain committed to eliminating foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism from the country.
Earlier, on October 18, 2026, security forces killed eight terrorists during intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts of Balochistan, ARY News reported, citing the ISPR.
According to the report, security forces conducted three IBOs in the districts following reports of the presence of terrorists affiliated with the Indian proxy Fitna Al Hindustan. The operations resulted in the killing of eight Indian-sponsored terrorists, the ISPR said.

title: Karachi man dies in ambulance while being shifted to hospital 43km away
text:
Karachi man dies in ambulance while being shifted to hospital 43km away
- By Salman Lodhi -
- Oct 19, 2026
KARACHI: A man injured in a suspected robbery attempt in Ghaghar Phatak died while being shifted to hospital after waiting on the road for medical assistance, ARY News reported.
According to police, the victim, identified as Abbas, was injured when armed robbers opened fire during a robbery resistance incident in Ghaghar Phatak.
Abbas reportedly remained on the road for a considerable time, waiting for an ambulance. People present at the scene were allegedly busy recording videos instead of helping the injured man.
An ambulance was eventually arranged to transport him to Jinnah Hospital, located around 43 kilometres away. However, Abbas died during the journey to the hospital.
Police said the initial investigation suggested that the shooting took place when the victim resisted a robbery attempt.
Meanwhile, a dead body found in a bag in Karachi’s Nazimabad has been identified.
“The deceased has been identified as Adnan,” police said. “The suspect, Nisar, has also been arrested with the help of the CCTV footage,” officials said.
“Accused Nisar has been a native of Badin district and working as a gardener at a nursery at KDA Chowrangi,” according to police.
“Deceased Adnan and the accused were working at the same nursery and were engaged in a personal feud for some time,” police said.
The murder victim Adnan had two days ago tied accused Nisar with rope and subjected him to bodily torture. Avenging personal grudge Nisar killed Adnan with blows of hammer and put the body in a bag and thrown it, according to police.

title: Arteta hails Arsenal 'finishers' after Madueke fells Forest
text:
Arteta hails Arsenal 'finishers' after Madueke fells Forest
- By AFP -
- Oct 19, 2026
Mikel Arteta said Arsenal’s strength in depth will be key to their Premier League title defence after Noni Madueke came off the bench to clinch a 1-0 win against Nottingham Forest on Sunday.
Arteta’s side were well below their best at the City Ground and did not register a shot on target until Madueke bagged their winner 10 minutes from full-time.
While the Gunners earned few style points in the east midlands, they will not be overly concerned after moving within three points of leaders Manchester City.
Arteta is able to dip into one of the stronger substitutes’ benches in the top-flight and he made full use of the resources at his disposal to turn the tide by the banks of the River Trent.
Crucially, he sent on Madueke for the underwhelming Eberechi Eze at half-time.
He also introduced Mikel Merino, Viktor Gyokeres and Jurrien Timber as the second half wore on.
It was Madueke who provided the key intervention, cutting in from the left flank to unleash a powerful drive that deflected past Forest keeper Matz Sels in the 80th minute.
“We had to earn it until the last second. They are a well coached team and hard to break down. We had to take risks, they are a dangerous team,” Arteta said.
“We had to manage the emotional part really well. We stayed focused and the finishers made a huge impact.”
Arsenal are in the midst of a hectic schedule which included a Champions League win over Lille in midweek and a looming European trip to Bayern Munich on Wednesday.
Arteta’s ability to rest key players without significantly weakening his team could be a major factor in the title race.
“Some of them played three days ago and some of them will start the next game and they know that everyone has to be at it,” he said.
“If you are needed after 60 minutes, 45 minutes and sometimes two minutes. We have a squad now that can deliver in moments and we have to use that.
“Noni, Jurrien, Mikel was brilliant when he came on and Viktor really changed the game, all of them did and that’s what we need.
“Noni obviously the highlight because he scored the goal and that’s the difference.”
After a shock 3-0 loss at Brighton on September 19, second-placed Arsenal have bounced back with three successive victories.
The north Londoners have not been able to recapture the relentless consistency that took them to a first title in 22 years last season.
But they retain the priceless ability to grind out wins and this was their sixth in seven league matches.
“Sometimes you can get frustrated with teams who are difficult to break down. First half we didn’t have a shot on target and that’s something we discussed,” Arteta said.
“We had another two big ones in the second half but the only one on target we had was a little deflection and it’s in.”

title: ‘Impose agricultural emergency in Pakistan,’ urges Kissan Ittehad president
text:
‘Impose agricultural emergency in Pakistan,’ urges Kissan Ittehad president
- By Web Desk -
- Oct 18, 2026
MULTAN: Pakistan Kissan Ittehad President Khalid Mahmood Khokhar has called for the imposition of an agricultural emergency in the country, saying delayed government decisions are causing repeated losses to farmers, ARY News reported.
Addressing a press conference in Multan, Khokhar said a loss in one crop affects the next three crops. He added that Pakistan was continuously falling behind in the agriculture sector and urged the government to take timely decisions.
He demanded a 25 per cent profit margin on production costs for farmers. He said farmers were not receiving fair prices for their crops because the government cited conditions imposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
Khokhar said people were struggling to obtain wheat and argued that farmers would cultivate more wheat if they received a fair price. He noted that the government had fixed the wheat price at Rs4,500 per maund.
The Kissan Ittehad president also said sugarcane growers had yet to receive an adequate price for their crop despite a 16 per cent increase in sugarcane production this year. He said sugarcane cultivation had reached an unprecedented level in the country’s history, leaving growers worried about their financial returns.
Khokhar recalled that sugarcane growers were exploited in 2017 when the government delayed sugar exports. He said the decision to export sugar came only after farmers had suffered financial losses.
He criticised the politicisation of agriculture in Pakistan, saying the sector needed timely decisions and consistent policies.
Khokhar said food security had become a top priority worldwide, while Pakistani leaders continued to politicise wheat and flour. He added that other countries were providing substantial subsidies to their agriculture sectors, while Pakistani farmers were struggling with rising production costs and inadequate crop prices.

title: Oman introduces 8-hour daily work limit
text:
Oman sets 8-hour daily work limit under Labour Law 2023
- By Sheeraz Soomro -
- Oct 18, 2026
MUSCAT: Oman’s Labour Law, issued under Royal Decree No. 53/2023, sets clear limits on working hours to safeguard employees’ health and well-being and promote workplace efficiency.
According to Article 70 of the law, employers cannot require employees to work more than eight hours a day or 40 hours a week. The law also provides for a one-hour break during the working day for rest and meals.
Employees must not be required to work for more than six consecutive hours without a break, according to the provisions outlined in the report.
Special provisions apply during the holy month of Ramadan. Muslim employees are entitled to reduced working hours, limited to a maximum of six hours a day or 30 hours a week.
The law also urged transparency in workplace schedules. Employers are required to display working hours and weekly rest days in a clearly visible location within the workplace.
Read more: Oman Labour Laws 2023: Complete guide for workplace dispute resolutions
The requirement is intended to ensure employees are informed about their work schedules and enable the relevant authorities to monitor compliance.
Under Oman Labour Law Royal Decree No. 53/2023, a structured and phased mechanism has been established for resolving disputes between workers and employers, aimed at ensuring justice, transparency, and timely resolution.
At the first stage, an internal grievance redressal system is mandatory at the institutional level. Under Article 8, establishments employing 50 or more workers are required to maintain a formal and approved complaints mechanism.
Through this system, employees may submit complaints directly or through a representative, allowing disputes to be addressed internally before legal proceedings become necessary.
If a matter cannot be resolved within the institution, the process moves to the administrative and judicial stage. Article 9 states that no labour case may be taken directly to court unless it has first been referred to the relevant department of the ministry for amicable settlement.
The concerned authority is required to attempt reconciliation within a maximum period of 30 days.

title: Cement and steel rates stabilize in Pakistan amid rising inflation
text:
Cement and steel rates stabilize in Pakistan amid rising inflation
- By Sher Muhammad -
- Oct 18, 2026
ISLAMABAD – The construction and real estate industry is adapting to a roller coaster economic scenario as the prices of basic building materials persisted at a steady plateau this week. The knee-jerk market fluctuations that were experienced during the past couple of months have subsided at least for now, but the overall procurement cost for cement and steel has frozen at a costly new normal.
Based on daily trade activity in key supply corridors from Lahore, Karachi and Islamabad; the grey cement pricing remains intact within the level of 1,500-1,610 Rs/50kg bag across different geographies owing to transport costs and brand specific manufacturing origin. Major players like Bestway, DG Khan, Maple Leaf and Lucky Cement are traded in the range of 1,515-1,590 Rs/50kg bag throughout general retail networks with about 1,700+ Rs/50kg bag being available for high value sulfate-resistant product. Regional prices haven’t deviated much with southern supplies cheaper by few Rupees/50kg bag closer to the seaport facilities and northern channels bearing some freight premium.
At the same time, domestic steel rebar prices, which had been “flat for the last several weeks,” have plateaued. Benchmark Grade 60 steel reinforcement bars, which are most commonly used to provide structural integrity for modern multi-storied buildings and housing complexes, are trading around 277 rupees ($4.28) per kilogram, or approximately 277,000 rupees ($4,283) per metric ton at mill-gate levels. Grade 40 steel reinforcement bar trades just behind at 275 rupees ($4.24) per kilogram, or approximately 275,000 rupees ($4,245) per metric ton. Steel rebar pricing has been unchanged due to imports of scrap metal flowing into the system in good volumes and stable inventory levels while the high cost of production limits downward movement.
What you see here are the immediate weekly numbers but what is also already visible is a structural change in Pakistan’s national building economy. Sustained inflation, depreciation and increasing utility tariff have adjusted the real estate development price for the one last few years. Long-term market monitoring shows that the grey cement, for example, which was selling for a little below Rs700/bag just five years ago has more than doubled, the price of the steel reinforcement bars has also increased by a similar proportion, aided by higher international scrap prices and domestic electricity tariff changes that directly impact the heavy induction melting and rolling mill process.
As for individual property owners this escalation represents a huge increase in the amount of capital necessary to build a standard grey structure (complete with foundation, walls and slabs). Industry rates state that even for a simple one storey 1,000sq foot residential layout 400-450 bags of cement are used for structural foundations, slabs and walling – ensuring individual property developers already need an upfront baseline outlay of over 650,000 rupees alone in cement alone at current pricing before steel re-bar and other consumables.
Consequently, the composite latest construction cost estimates for contemporary complete construction-structural grey work along with basic interior finishing-now hovers in the range of 3,000-3,250 rupees per square foot for city markets. Standard five-marla typical private dwelling comprising gross construction area of around 1,350 square feet now often necessitate a minimum investment of anywhere from 5.5 million to 8.5 million rupees (without GST), according to industrial standards, while scaled-up standalone ten-marla and one-kanal homes are substantially higher in the double-digit range of tens of millions of rupees, Industry specialists recommend that builders verify fresh bills of quantities and reconcile weighbridge slips firsthand with principal leading dealers to trade better through the buildup scenario.

title: Abbottabad
text:
Abbottabad is a city and the capital of the Hazara Division in the Pakistani province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. It also serves as the headquarters of its eponymous tehsil (subdistrict) and district. According to the 2023 census, Abbottabad had a population of 234,395. The city is located about 120 km (75 mi) north of the Islamabad–Rawalpindi area and 150 km (95 mi) east of Peshawar, at an elevation of about 1,256 m (4,121 ft).
Abbottabad was founded in 1853 during British rule and was named after James Abbott, the first deputy commissioner of Hazara. It developed as a cantonment and administrative centre in the colonial period, later becoming part of the North-West Frontier Province and then Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Parts of the city are administered as Abbottabad Cantonment, while the wider urban area also includes municipal administration.
The city is associated with education, healthcare, tourism and military institutions. It is home to institutions such as Ayub Medical College and the Abbottabad campus of COMSATS University Islamabad, while the Pakistan Military Academy is located at nearby Kakul. Abbottabad also serves as a market and transit centre for surrounding areas of the Hazara region and as a base for travel to nearby hill stations and destinations in northern Pakistan, including the Galyat region and the Kaghan Valley.


Etymology
The name Abbottabad combines the name of the city's founder, James Abbott, with the Persian-derived suffix ābād, meaning an inhabited place, settlement or town. The name therefore means "Abbott's town". Abbottabad is one of two Pakistani cities commonly cited as being named after British army officers, the other being Jacobabad.


History


Early history and founding
Before the colonial era, the area now occupied by Abbottabad formed part of rural Hazara. From the mid-18th to the early 19th centuries, the area was under the Durrani Empire, and it came under the Sikh Empire in 1820 when the region was conquered by forces led by Hari Singh Nalwa. Haripur, founded by Nalwa in 1822, became the capital of Hazara before the establishment of Abbottabad.
Following the Second Anglo-Sikh War, the East India Company annexed the Punjab region up to Peshawar. James Abbott, a British officer in the Bengal Army, served as deputy commissioner of Hazara from 1847 to 1853. In January 1853, during his tenure, Abbott founded the town that became Abbottabad. The name, meaning Abbott's town, was adopted at the suggestion of Herbert Edwardes, another East India Company officer and administrator.

Abbottabad replaced Haripur as the headquarters of Hazara District and developed as an administrative and military centre. During this period, Hazara and much of what is now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa formed part of British India's Punjab Province. Abbott later wrote the poem Abbottabad, which expressed his attachment to the town before his departure from India. A marble version of the poem is displayed in Lady Garden Park.


British period
After the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the province passed from East India Company rule to the direct rule of the British Crown, and Abbottabad remained a military cantonment. During the rebellion, the 4th Sikhs, who had been stationed at Abbottabad, marched towards Ludhiana to prevent rebels from Jullundur crossing the Sutlej. In 1867, following conflict in the Black Mountain area, the Khan of Agror was taken into British custody and sent to Abbottabad.
The town and cantonment grew during the later 19th century. The 1881 census recorded a population of 4,189 people living in 918 houses, with about two-thirds of the population in the cantonment and about one-third in the civil station. Abbottabad also served as a base for military activity connected with the Black Mountain expeditions of 1888 and 1891.
On 9 November 1901, Lord Curzon, the British governor-general of India, established the North-West Frontier Province from the north-western districts of the Punjab, making Abbottabad part of the new province. In the early 20th century, Abbottabad was a military cantonment and sanatorium, and served as the headquarters of a brigade in the Second Division of the Northern Army Corps. The garrison included Frontier Force infantry, Gurkha battalions and mountain batteries.
In 1901, the population of Abbottabad town and cantonment was 7,764. It rose to 11,506 by 1911. Public institutions recorded in the early 20th century included Anglo-Vernacular schools and a government dispensary. On 24 August 1945, Jawaharlal Nehru, later the first prime minister of India, addressed a public meeting in Abbottabad after hearing of the death of Subhas Chandra Bose.


Post-independence
Before the partition of British India, a referendum was held in the North-West Frontier Province to decide whether the province would join India or Pakistan; the result was in favour of joining Pakistan. After independence in 1947, the Pakistan Military Academy was established at Kakul, near Abbottabad, for the training of Pakistan Army officers. In June 1948, the British Red Cross opened a hospital in Abbottabad to treat people injured during the conflict in Kashmir.
In 1955, Abbottabad and the rest of the North-West Frontier Province became part of West Pakistan under the One Unit Scheme. The province was restored in 1970 under the Legal Framework Order, 1970, and Hazara later became a division with Abbottabad as its headquarters. The North-West Frontier Province was renamed Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in 2010 after the Eighteenth Amendment to the Constitution of Pakistan.


Recent history
Abbottabad was affected by the 2005 Kashmir earthquake. Most of the city survived, but many older buildings were destroyed or damaged, and the city received people displaced from Azad Kashmir after the earthquake. In 2009 and 2010, Abbottabad also received internally displaced people from Swat District and Waziristan during military operations against militants.
On 25 January 2011, Indonesian militant Umar Patek, a member of Jemaah Islamiyah, was arrested in Abbottabad. He was wanted in connection with the Christmas Eve 2000 Indonesia bombings and the 2002 Bali bombings.
On 2 May 2011, Abbottabad gained international attention when United States forces killed Osama bin Laden in his compound in the city during the Abbottabad raid. Pakistani authorities demolished the compound in February 2012.


Demographics
Population
According to the 2023 census, Abbottabad had a population of 234,395, consisting of 159,683 people in Abbottabad Cantonment and 74,712 people in Abbottabad Municipal Committee. The same census listed Nawan Shehr and Murree Gallies Cantonment as separate urban localities in Abbottabad District.
Historical census figures show growth from 4,189 people in 1881. The population decreased between 1891 and 1901, and increased notably by 1941 during World War II. Historical figures are affected by changes in administrative boundaries and census definitions.


Religion
The 2023 census religion tables are published by district, tehsil and rural–urban classification rather than by each individual urban locality. In urban Abbottabad Tehsil, Islam was the largest reported religion in 2023, followed by Christianity.


Languages

According to the 2023 census, Hindko was the most commonly reported mother tongue in urban Abbottabad Tehsil, spoken by 75.39% of the population. Pashto was reported by 14.08%, Urdu by 5.28%, Punjabi by 2.60%, Kohistani by 0.86% and other languages of Pakistan by 1.79%.


Geography
Abbottabad is located in the Hazara Division of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, northern Pakistan. The city lies north of the Islamabad–Rawalpindi metropolitan area and east of Peshawar, in the hill country between the plains of the Indus River and the mountain routes leading towards northern Pakistan and Kashmir. It is situated at an elevation of about 1,256 m (4,121 ft) on a plateau at the southern end of the Rash, or Orash, Plain.
A 2024 sustainable mobility study described Abbottabad as lying in the Orash Valley at about 1,250 m (4,100 ft) above sea level, in the foothills of the Hindu Kush and Karakoram ranges. The city lies on road routes connecting the plains of the Indus River, the Kashmir region and northern Pakistan. Havelian, about 16 km (9.9 mi) south of Abbottabad, is the nearest railhead.
The surrounding district contains mountainous and forested terrain. A 2004 strategy prepared by IUCN Pakistan and the Government of the North-West Frontier Province reported that forests covered about 20% of Abbottabad District and accounted for 5.4% of the province's forest resources, although the district made up 1.8% of the province's land area. The same strategy identified soil erosion and watershed management as environmental concerns in the district, and recorded seven sub-watersheds, of which three were then covered by regular watershed programmes. These figures refer to Abbottabad District rather than only the municipal city.


Climate
Abbottabad has a humid subtropical climate under the Köppen climate classification. Climate-Data.org gives Abbottabad an average annual temperature of 15.9 °C (60.6 °F) and average annual rainfall of 1,532 mm (60.3 in). Average temperatures are lowest in January and highest in June. Rainfall occurs throughout the year, with the highest monthly totals in July and August during the summer monsoon period.


Economy
Abbottabad functions as a market centre for Abbottabad District. Its local economy is closely linked with services, education, tourism and its role as an administrative centre. At the district level, the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Board of Investment and Trade identifies hospitality and tourism, education, mining and mineral development as sectors in which Abbottabad District has comparative advantages.
Tourism forms an important part of the local economy. A working paper by the Pakistan Institute of Development Economics described tourism as a major component of Abbottabad city's economy and noted that the city also serves as a transit point for other destinations in northern Pakistan. The same study reported that tourism-related activity was associated with local pressures including traffic congestion, price fluctuations, littering and noise pollution.
In the wider district, economic activity includes subsistence agriculture, livestock and poultry rearing, forestry-related livelihoods, mining and small-scale industry. A fact sheet prepared in connection with IUCN's environmental fiscal reform work in Abbottabad described subsistence agriculture as the mainstay of the district economy, with additional household income from backyard poultry and livestock rearing. The same source stated that mining in the district was limited, despite identified mineral deposits, and was mainly dominated by soapstone and limestone. These descriptions refer to Abbottabad District rather than only the municipal city.


Government and administration
Abbottabad is the administrative centre of Abbottabad District and hosts several divisional and district offices. The district administration lists the offices of the Commissioner of Hazara Division, the Deputy Inspector General of Hazara Division, the Station Commander, the Military Estate Officer, the Deputy Commissioner of Abbottabad and the District Police Officer among government offices working in the district.
District administration in Abbottabad is organised under the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa local government framework. According to an audit report by the Auditor General of Pakistan, district government activities are managed through the office of the Deputy Commissioner and district officers, including officers for education, health, agriculture, fisheries, population welfare, sports, livestock and dairy development, cooperation and social welfare.
Abbottabad District is divided into four tehsils: Abbottabad, Havelian, Lower Tanawal and Lora. Tehsil municipal administrations are managed by tehsil municipal officers, assisted by officers for finance, regulation and infrastructure. Their functions include preparing local development plans, managing municipal services and infrastructure, exercising control over land use and zoning, regulating markets and services, issuing licences and permits, collecting local taxes and organising cultural and recreational events.
Parts of Abbottabad are administered separately as Abbottabad Cantonment. The 2023 census counted Abbottabad Cantonment and Abbottabad Municipal Committee as separate urban localities. Cantonments in Pakistan are administered under the cantonment system; the Cantonments Act, 1924 provides for a cantonment board and an executive officer for every cantonment.
Municipal water and sanitation services are also handled through a separate public service company. A performance audit report by the Auditor General of Pakistan states that the Water and Sanitation Services Company Abbottabad was established by the Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in April 2017, with water supply functions transferred from tehsil municipal administrations to the company through a services and asset management agreement.


Tourism
Abbottabad has long been associated with summer tourism because of its hill-station setting and its location on routes into northern Pakistan. Encyclopaedia Britannica describes Abbottabad as a hill station and a summer resort, and identifies it as a gateway to the Kaghan Valley. The Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Culture and Tourism Authority describes the city as a summer resort in a spacious valley about 1,250 m (4,100 ft) above sea level.
The city also serves as a base for travel to nearby hill stations and natural areas in Abbottabad District and the wider Galyat region. A travel guide published by the Pakistan Tourism Development Corporation describes Abbottabad as a base for trips to the Kaghan Valley and the Gallies, and lists Shimla Hill and Ilyasi Masjid among places to visit in Abbottabad city. The same guide identifies Harnoi as a picnic spot about 10 km (6.2 mi) northeast of Abbottabad on the main Nathia Gali road.
Nathia Gali can be approached from both Murree and Abbottabad, and is about 38 km (24 mi) from each. Ayubia National Park, located in Abbottabad District, was declared a national park on 17 January 1984 and covers about 3,375 ha (8,340 acres). Other nearby destinations include Thandiani, which KP Tourism describes as a hill resort about 30 km (19 mi) east of Abbottabad at an altitude of about 2,800 m (9,200 ft).
The wider Galyat area includes several trekking routes. The Galyat brochure lists routes including Nathia Gali to Mushkpuri, Dungagali to Ayubia, and Nathia Gali to Miranjani.

Abbottabad's road links also connect it with long-distance tourist routes into northern Pakistan. The Karakoram Highway connects Islamabad with Kashgar in Xinjiang, China, and passes through or near the Hindu Kush and Karakoram ranges. As a result, Abbottabad is often used as a transit point for travel towards the mountain valleys and towns of northern Pakistan.
Tourism in Abbottabad District is seasonal. A working paper by the Pakistan Institute of Development Economics identified June to August as peak tourist months in the district, with March to May and September to October treated as normal tourist months and November to February as a lower-tourism period. The same study reported that tourism-related activity was associated with local pressures including traffic congestion, price increases, littering and noise pollution.


Culture and landmarks

Abbottabad's cultural landscape includes colonial-era civic buildings, religious sites, public gardens and museum collections associated with the wider Hazara region. The district administration lists several historical, archaeological and tourist attractions in Abbottabad, including Abbott House, St. Luke's Church, the Catholic Church, the Old Tehsil Building and Abbott Museum.
St. Luke's Church is one of the city's main surviving colonial-era religious buildings. The church was built in 1864 during British rule and was originally established to serve British officials in the Indian subcontinent. The church has retained features from its early period, including stained-glass windows, old locks, a pipe organ and memorial plaques.
Lady Garden Park is another colonial-era landmark associated with the city's early history. A marble plaque in the park contains the poem Abbottabad, written by James Abbott, after whom the city is named.
Abbottabad also has museum collections connected with the archaeology and ethnology of the Hazara region. The Hazara University Department of Archaeology states that it runs Abbott Museum in Abbottabad and Hazara University Museum, and that the museums contain archaeological and ethnological materials acquired through explorations, excavations, purchases and donations. The Directorate General of Archaeology and Museums, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa also lists Abbottabad Museum among the museums managed by the provincial archaeology department.
Ilyasi Masjid in Nawan Shehr is a religious and cultural landmark of Abbottabad. The mosque was built around 1927–1932 and is located near a natural stream at the foot of a hill. Visit Silk Road describes it as a historical place in Nawan Shehr and states that it was built on a mountain spring in 1932.


Education

Abbottabad has a concentration of school-level, higher-education and professional institutions in the Hazara Division. The district administration describes the city as a "city of schools and colleges" because of its public and private schools, colleges and universities. The University of Engineering & Technology, Peshawar has also described Abbottabad as having gained fame as a city of schools and colleges.
At the district level, a report by the Auditor General of Pakistan recorded 1,317 primary, 165 middle, 123 secondary and 30 higher secondary schools in Abbottabad District, and gave the district literacy rate as 56.6%. The same report recorded enrolment of 135,494 students in boys' government schools and 118,258 students in girls' government schools in the district. These figures refer to Abbottabad District rather than only the municipal city.
School-level institutions in and around Abbottabad include Army Burn Hall College, Abbottabad Public School, Pakistan International Public School and College and Army Public School and College, PMA Kakul campus.
The city includes several higher-education and professional institutions. COMSATS University Islamabad operates an Abbottabad campus; the Higher Education Commission lists Abbottabad among the university's campuses. The University of Engineering & Technology, Peshawar operates an Abbottabad Campus, which was inaugurated in October 2002 in the former premises of Ayub Medical College. The campus lists departments and programmes in fields including electronics engineering, architecture, city and regional planning, computer science and software engineering.
Ayub Medical College, a public medical college in Abbottabad, opened its first academic year on 15 May 1979 and later moved to its Mansehra Road campus in 1990. The Pakistan Medical and Dental Council lists Abbottabad International Medical College, Frontier Medical College and Women Medical College among private medical colleges in Abbottabad.
Pakistan Military Academy is located at Kakul, about 8 km (5.0 mi) northeast of Abbottabad, and provides officer training for the Pakistan Army.


Healthcare
Abbottabad is a healthcare centre for the Hazara Division and surrounding areas of northern Pakistan. Public health services in Abbottabad District include primary and secondary facilities administered through district health authorities. A report by the Auditor General of Pakistan for audit year 2021–22 recorded 108 health facilities across the district, including 54 basic health units, 42 civil dispensaries, five rural health centres and three tehsil headquarters or Category-D hospitals. The same report stated that the Department of Health used an Independent Monitoring Unit to monitor health facility performance through field-based data collection and district monitoring officers. These figures refer to Abbottabad District rather than only the municipal city.
Ayub Medical and Teaching Institution, Abbottabad is a major tertiary care teaching hospital associated with Ayub Medical College. The hospital began working in 1995 and reached 1,000-bed status in 1998. Its services include outpatient and inpatient care, general and specialised wards, accident and emergency care, intensive and cardiac care units, operation theatres, delivery suites, pharmacy, radiology and imaging, physiotherapy, blood bank and laboratory services. The institution states that its catchment area includes the Hazara Division, Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Kashmir.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, a study of healthcare workers in hospitals of Abbottabad found that the pandemic negatively affected their quality of life. In December 2020, a data from the National Command and Operation Centre, reported that Abbottabad had recorded the highest COVID-19 positivity ratio in Pakistan on reported dates that month.


Sports
Cricket is one of the main organised sports associated with Abbottabad. Abbottabad Cricket Stadium, is listed by the Pakistan Cricket Board as a first-class cricket ground. The ground has been used for domestic cricket; the PCB's 2024–25 Quaid-e-Azam Trophy schedule included matches at Abbottabad Cricket Stadium.
Abbottabad has been represented in Pakistan's domestic cricket structure by regional teams. The Pakistan Cricket Board listed Abbottabad Region among the teams in the 2024–25 Quaid-e-Azam Trophy. The former Abbottabad Falcons also appeared in national domestic cricket records, including Twenty20 and List A cricket competitions.
The city also has facilities for field hockey. In 2021, the Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had approved funds for reconstruction of Abbottabad Hockey Stadium, including installation of AstroTurf, floodlights, a sprinkler system, spectator stands and other improvements.


Transport

Abbottabad is connected by road with the plains of the Indus River and the Kashmir region, and by rail through nearby Havelian. Its position on routes between central Pakistan and the northern highlands has made the city an important transport point for movement towards northern Pakistan and areas along the Karakoram Highway.
The Karakoram Highway is the principal interregional road corridor associated with Abbottabad. The highway connects Kashgar in Xinjiang, China, with Islamabad, Pakistan, and passes through or near the Hindu Kush and Karakoram mountain ranges. A 2024 sustainable mobility study identified the Karakoram Highway as the main corridor for the first phase of a proposed bus rapid transit line in Abbottabad.
A 2024 sustainable urban mobility factsheet reported that walking accounted for 64% of trips in the Abbottabad urban area, followed by informal public transport at 16%, formal public transport at 5%, private cars at 6%, private motorcycles or two-wheelers at 5%, and other modes at 4%. The same source identified major urban mobility issues in the city, including vehicle inflows linked to tourism, commercial traffic passing through the city, limited alternative routes and parking areas, weak facilities for non-motorised transport, road-safety problems and vehicle-related air pollution.
The nearest railway station is Havelian railway station in Havelian, about 16 km (9.9 mi) south of Abbottabad, which connects the area with Peshawar through the Pakistan Railways network.


Notes


References


External links

title: Ahmedpur East
text:
Ahmedpur East (also known as Ahmadpur Sharqia) is a city located in Bahawalpur District in Punjab province of Pakistan. As of the 2023 census, the city has a population of approximately 196,618, making it the 69th most populous city in Pakistan. The city is situated near the Cholistan Desert, offering a hot desert climate with extreme summers and mild winters. 
Ahmedpur East was built by Ahmed Khan son of Qadir Din Khan and grandson of Piruj Khan, in 1748. The city was badly damaged by heavy floods from the Ghara River in 1758. A new city on a mound half a mile to the south of the previous site was selected for the present city.


Demographics
Population

According to 2023 census, Ahmedpur East had a population of 196,618.
Languages


Culture
The city of Ahmedpur East is a tourist destination for not only locals but provides an important hot spot for historians and archaeologists due to its rich heritage. The city contains the Sadiq Garh Palace and many old buildings which were built by Nawab Sadiq I. The Derawar Fort is also in Ahmedpur East Tehsil. Ahmedpur East is also known for its cotton, silk, embroidery, carpets, and extraordinarily delicate pottery.


Nuclear power plant
According to The Wall Street Journal, Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission (PAEC) plans to install three Chinese nuclear reactors at Ahmedpur East and the site is now being prepared. The Ahmedpur East nuclear power complex would have 1100 MW nuclear reactor.


2017 oil tanker fire disaster

In 2017, Ahmedpur East was the site of a major disaster, when over 200 villagers collecting fuel from an overturned truck were killed in an accidental explosion. More than 70 among the injured died in burn centers. Updated numbers indicate that at least 200 people died in the explosion.
The death toll of Ahmadpur East oil tanker tragedy reached to 219 when another victim died at the Nishtar Hospital, Multan.
As many as 94 victims died in different hospitals, including 18 at Jinnah Hospital, Lahore, 11 at Burns Ward of CMH, Bahawalpur, and 10 at Bahawal Victoria Hospital. However, 34 injured persons were under treatment at different hospitals, including 22 at BVH, five at THQ Hospital, Ahmadpur East, three at Nishtar Hospital, Multan, and four at Jinnah Hospital, Lahore.
According to the focal person appointed for giving details about the tragedy Dr. Amir Mahmood, 31 injured persons had been discharged after recovery. Meanwhile, relatives of several Ahmadpur East tragedy victims alleged that their financial aid cheque issued by the district government on the order of Punjab CM Shahbaz Sharif had been bounced by the banks concerned. The DC Office spokesman through the Information Department said that the claim was not true. The spokesperson said that if any cheque did not cash then the concerned families should immediately contact the DC Office.


Education Facilities in Ahmedpur East
Apart from the Abbas Higher Secondary School and Army Public School at Dera Nawab Sahib, the city has two government postgraduate colleges. The city also has a government commerce college, Government Sadiq Abbas Degree College and a college for individuals who require special education. 
Many private colleges such as Punjab College, Nimz College, Allama Iqbal College, United College, Millat College, Laurel College, City College, Oxford College, Amal College and many more are working there. A campus of the Virtual University of Pakistan is also situated here. There are about ten government high schools in the city and nearby area. 
The city contains hundreds of private schools. Some of them are Allied School, Islamic Model Higher Secondary School, Country School System, The Educators, Dr AQ School System, The Smart School, Dar-e-Arqam School, EFA School System, The PACE School System and many more.


Shrines of Sufi saints
Syed Mohammad Abdullah Shah Madni Jilani, great grand son of Abdul Rehman Jilani Dehlvi and a descendant of Sheikh Abdul Qadir Gilani. Born and raised in Medina, he walked miles between Mecca and Medina in the heat. He then spent least 12 years of service at the Prophet's Mosque and had a dream where Prophet Muhammad ordered him to find his murshid Sultan Bahu. He met Sultan Bahu during the reign of Nawab Bahawal Khan III, he migrated from Medina to Ahmadpur East for a permanent residence from 6 May 1826. He died on 20 April 1860. His shrine is situated at Fatani Chowk, Fatani Street, Ahmadpur East. He is the 26th Shaikh of the Sarwari Qadiri Sufi order.
Makhdoom Bahauddin Akbar, belonging to Bahauddin Zakariya's 18th generation of descendants. He migrated from Multan to Ahmadpur East. He died on 24 January 1851. He belonged to the Suhrawardiyya order.
Azmat Sultan, a descendant of Sultan Bahu. His father, Sultan Mohammad Hussain was a Sufi dervish. Azmat Sultan migrated to Ahmadpur East along with his family and resided there. It was here that he died and his shrine is also located here.
Abdul Asad Khan Afghan: There is a khanqah by the name of Abdul Asad Khan in Ahmadpur East. He is known as being the khalifah of Khawaja Aaqil Mohammad.
Noor Shah Bukhari: His shrine is located near Qilla Tehsil. He is from the progeny of Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari. He spent most of his time in the Zikr of Allah. The order of his followers initiated in the desert area.
Molvi Hakeem Gul Mohammad: His khanqah exists in Ahmadpur East. His family was prominent for its knowledge and herbal tips. The shrines of his ancestors still exist in Multan and Uch, Pakistan. He was the khalifah and a disciple of Aaqil Mohammad. His family lineage and biography is preserved in his writing Takmala Sharif.
Khawaja Muhammad Abdul Malik Siddique was the Peer-e-Tariqat of Naqshbandi-Haqqani Golden Chain. Khawaja Muhammad Abdul Malik Siddique was the khalifa of Peer Shaikh Mufti Muhammad Fareed Sahib and of Peer Fazal Ali Qureshi of Miskeen Pur Sharif, Muzaffargarh District. Now his son Khawaja Abdul Majid Siddiqui is the Sajjada Nashin of Khanqah Malikia.
Molana Manzoor Ahmed Faizi was a scholar and Sufi from the Chishtia order.


Abbasi Mosque
Abbasi Mosque, situated nearby, is a historical and significant mosque. This mosque was established in the year 1804 by Haji Allah Ditta Khoker, who laid its foundation stone. The design of Abbasiya Masjid closely resembles that of the famous Derawar Mosque, which is renowned for its grandeur and unique structure.
The mosque is known for its architecture and intricate details that make it a place of both spiritual significance and aesthetic appeal. Its spacious prayer hall is designed to accommodate a large number of worshippers, making it a central hub for the local Muslim community. In addition to the prayer space, the mosque features several important facilities, including a madrasa (Islamic school), where students are taught religious education, and a wuzu (ablution) area, which allows worshippers to perform the necessary ritual washing before prayers. There are also modern washrooms available for the convenience of the visitors.
Abbasiya Masjid has the capacity to accommodate almost 20,000 people for prayer.
The mosque is led by its imam, Qari Bashir Ahmed.


Ghalla Mandi
The Ghalla Mandi in Ahmedpur East is a major agricultural marketplace, where farmers, traders, and vendors come together to buy and sell various commodities, particularly cotton. Located in the central region of the city, it plays a vital role in the local economy, serving as a hub for the agricultural community. The mandi is known for its bustling atmosphere, with a diverse range of goods being exchanged, including cotton, grains, and other produce.


References

title: Attock
text:
Attock (Punjabi, Urdu: اٹک) is a city in Punjab, Pakistan, not far from the national capital Islamabad. The headquarters of the Attock District, it is the 36th largest city in the Punjab and the 61st largest city in the country, by population. The city was founded in 1908 several miles southeast of the historical city of Attock Khurd, which had been established by the Mughal emperor Akbar in the 16th century, and was initially named in honour of Sir Colin Campbell.


Etymology
The name 'Attock' is the romanised form of the Punjabi word aṭak, which means 'blockade, barrier or obstruction', although it is also translated as 'skirt of the mountains', owing to the hilly landscape of the district. The city was initially founded by the Mughal emperor Akbar as Atak-Banāras (Urdu: اٹک بنارس). It was named Campbellpur after the Commander-in-Chief of British forces Sir Colin Campbell, who rebuilt the city. The name 'Attock' was revived in 1978.


Demographics


Population

According to 2023 census, Attock had a population of 176,544.


Language

In the 2023 census 62.44% of the population spoke Punjabi, 15.58% spoke Pashto, 12.22% spoke Urdu, 2.11% spoke Hindko, 1.19% spoke Saraiki, while 1.32% spoke other national languages of Pakistan (mostly Sindhi and Kashmiri). Another 5.14% of the population chose "Others" for their mother tongue.


Geography
Attock is located east of the Indus River, in the Pothohar Plateau, Geographically, the district is mainly hills, plateaus and river/stream dissected plains. The Indus River flows on the Northern and Western borders of the district. After Haripur, the Haro River passes through the North of the tehsil of Attock where there is a floodplain with fertile soil between 2 mountain ranges, this is where Attock city itself is located. Elevation varies with many of the plains being 300-600m above sea level while the hills and ranges reach upwards of 1200m above sea level. The range south of the city is called the Kala Chitta Mountain Range while the one north of the city is known as Gandghar.
The city is located at a distance of 80 km (50 mi) from Rawalpindi, 100 km (62 mi) from Peshawar, and 10 km (6 mi) from the Pakistan Aeronautical Complex, Kamra.


History


Ancient period
Attock is located in the historical region of Gandhara. Alexander the Great, Mahmud of Ghazni, Timur, Nader Shah and Babur crossed the Indus at or about this spot (Attock Fort) in their invasions of Indian subcontinent.
After the founding of the city by the Mughal emperor Akbar, the construction of Attock Fort was completed in 1583 under the supervision of Khawaja Shamsuddin, a minister of Akbar. During the Mughal era, Attock was part of the Lahore Subah of Punjab.

Nader Shah crossed through Attock when he defeated the Mughals at the Battle of Karnal and thus ended Mughal power in Northern India.
Attock was then occupied by the Marathas in 1758 but this conquest was short-lived as Ahmad Shah Durrani came in person to recapture Attock and checked the Maratha advance after destroying their forces at Panipat. The Sikh Empire (1799–1849) under maharaja Ranjit Singh (1780–1839) captured the fortress of Attock in 1813 from the Durrani Nawab. After the occupation of Kashmir by Sikh Empire in 1820 many Kashmiris migrated to the plains of Attock.
In February 1849, Attock Khurd (Old Attock) was conquered by the British East India Company who created Campbellpur District. Following the Indian Rebellion in 1857, the region's strategic value was appreciated by the British, who established the Campbellpur Cantonment in 1857–58.


Modern Period
The Campbellpur Cantonment was established by the British colonial rulers in 1858. Campbellpur District was organised in 1904, by the division of Talagang Tehsil in the Jhelum District with the Pindigheb, Fateh Jang and Attock tehsils from Rawalpindi District. Today the Attock district consists of six tehsils: Fateh Jang, Hazro, Hassan Abdal, Jand, and Pindi Gheb.
The city's foundations were laid in 1908 and the city was named after Sir Colin Campbell, British Commander-in-Chief of India. The old city was established near the 16th century near the Attock fort that had guarded the major routes between Central Asia and South Asia. Attock's first oil well was drilled in Khaur in 1915, while the Attock Oil Company was established with a selling arrangement with the Burmah Oil Company. During 1928, the region produced 350,000 barrels of oil.
Attock was one of the northernmost points of the Punjab Province of British India prior to the partition; it thus found itself being a part of the common Hindi-Urdu phrase used to describe the length of colonial India: "Attock se Cuttack" (from Attock to Cuttack). The term "Attock se Cuttack" was first used to describe the extent of the Maratha Empire after they conquered Cuttack in 1750 and Attock in 1758.
After the independence of Pakistan in 1947, Hindu and Sikh minorities emigrated to India, while Muslim refugees from India settled in Attock. The Government of Pakistan renamed Campbellpur as Attock in 1978. The city and surrounding area are known for their high representation among soldiers of the Pakistan Army.


Education
According to the Alif Ailaan Pakistan District Education Rankings 2019, Attock is ranked 3 out of 146 districts of Pakistan in terms of the quality of education. For facilities and infrastructure, the district is ranked 17 out of 146. A detailed picture of the district's education performance is also available online.
Notable institutions include:- 

Air University Aerospace and Aviation Campus Kamra
COMSATS University Islamabad


Notable people


Climate
Attock has a humid subtropical climate (Köppen: Cwa) which has hot and humid summers, and cold to mild winters.


Sports

Indus Golf Club
PAC Golf Club
